Mr. Speaker, almost two weeks ago, on October 18, I rose and asked you to rule on whether or not the privileges of myself and other members have been breached by the boycott of the transport committee. While you continue to deliberate on that issue, I would like to raise a second related question of privilege.
I ask you to look at the failure of the government Whip to call an organizational meeting, as provided for in paragraph 579 in Beauchesne's Fifth Edition. It is only through his action that the committee can elect a chair and operate as the House intended when it struck the standing committee.
I ask you to rule on whether this failure to act impedes members of the House in the performance of their general duties on committee and, in particular, whether it prevents members of this House from performing the specific duty of reviewing the Order in Council appointments of two important transport officials. My arguments that there is prima facie case of privilege will be very brief.
A few years ago the House examined the operations of the House with a specific goal of increasing the role of private members. The Special Committee on Reform of the House, chaired by the former member, James McGrath, made several suggestions which were adopted by the House. Among these suggestions was a mechanism to enable House committees to review Order in
Council appointments. This empowerment of House committees provided for an accountability of the executive power to appoint and thus a check on abuse of patronage appointments.
The Standing Orders which govern the procedure are 110 and 111. Briefly, these rules provide that Order in Council appointments shall be tabled in the House within five days of their being gazetted and that they are automatically referred to a standing committee. The committee then has 30 days to make a decision on whether or not to summon the appointee and, if it decides to do so, a further 10 days to hold a hearing.
I do not think I can understate how important this right of review is to the proper functioning of Parliament. It is the only mechanism available to Canadians, as Standing Order 111(2) states, to "examine the qualifications and competence of the appointee or nominee to perform the duties of the post to which he or she has been appointed or nominated".
Yesterday, the government tabled two Order in Council appointments and referred them both to the Standing Committee on Transport. One is the appointment of the Deputy Minister of Transport, the other is the appointment of the Associate Deputy Minister of Transport. These are extremely important appointments. These two individuals will be charged with the day-to-day operations of one of our largest government departments. Yet, as things currently stand, I will be unable to ask the transport committee to summon these two important individuals. The committee will not be able to make a decision to summon them or not. The House of Commons will not be able to ask them to demonstrate their ability to meet the requirements of this public office.
It may be submitted that the government has another 28 days to call a meeting of the transport committee in order to enable it to review these appointments. I think there is evidence that they do not wish to call such a meeting.
Yesterday, the government introduced a motion to refer an important transport matter, the issue of open skies, to a special committee of the House. I was party to

October 30, 1990
Privilege
the original negotiations to refer this to the Standing Committee on Transport. Surely, if the standing committee were to meet soon, the government would have continued with its original plan.
In conclusion, I submit that the following establishes a prima facie case that the ability of members to fulfil their roles and responsibilities is being impeded by the chief government Whip. First, the Standing Committee on Transport is not meeting and cannot meet until the government Whip calls an organizational meeting. Second, the motion to establish a Special Committee on Transport is evidence of their intention to not call a meeting of the Standing Committee on Transport. Third, the appointments of the deputy minister and associate deputy minister have been referred to the Standing Committee on Transport. Fourth, until the Transport Committee meets, organizes, and elects a chair, I nor any other member of the House can ask for these appointees to come to committee. And, fifth, there is every indication that these appointments thus not be reviewed.
I apologize for taking up so much of your time, and the time of the House. I hope with your guidance, this entire matter can be resolved. If you find there is prima facie evidence, I would be delighted to introduce a motion to refer the matter to committee, in this case, not the Standing Committee on Transport.

-within the first ten sitting days after the Monday following Labour Day, lists of Members to compose the standing committees of the House and to act for the House on standing joint committees -
That is a responsibility which the committee I chair has and we met that obligation and reported to the House on October 5. Standing Order 104(l)(b) states that we may not report to the House again any earlier than the end of this calendar year.
We have a single report from the committee. The Standing Order says that can be the only report for this fall session related to the composition of committees of the House. We have done that.

*
October 30, 1990

I sought the unanimous consent and in all of our parliamentary history that has always been given for the formation of new committees, up until this fall. The McGrath committee report on reform of Parliament indicated that this should happen once a year so that members' privileges related to their membership on committees are protected and protected adequately, and that was done. But Standing Order 104 also states that we should have an opportunity to change those committees at the commencement of the fall session, each year. That is what should be happening in the House.
If we need to divide, that is fine. We should be dividing on that Striking Committee report. That is the remedy not only for the transport committee and the issues raised by the New Democratic Party Whip, but for some other situations as well that are becoming somewhat burdensome for members on all sides of the House.
During the course of the summer it is not unusual for opposition parties to change critics, as an example. It is not unusual for governments to change parliamentary secretaries and/or cabinet and responsibilities of one kind or another. That is what the summer in part, traditionally, has been for. If you look back on the attendance of those committees for the last couple of years, you will find that the poorest attendance relates to the committees that have been large. The best attendance relates to the committees that have been small.
I think you will find in particular that the obligation to be in attendance in the large committees has not been fulfilled more often by the opposition members than by government members. Attendance difficulty relates to their caucus and their sense of responsibility. We have had one other departure from normal over the summer, Mr. Speaker, in that we now have an abnormally large number of independents in the House. There are 13. We did our best as a striking committee. If the opposition members who spoke earlier this day would like to divide on that committee report right now or later when we are called to the House perhaps for another division later this day, at any convenient time government members would be quite prepared to face that division, and if the committee report were affirmed, we would be off with the new committees. It is incorrect, Mr. Speaker, to say that my action constitutes the remedy for the dilemma which the New Democratic Party proposes. speechtext:
that Bill C-83, an Act to revise and amend the law governing federal trust and loan companies and to provide for related and consequential matters, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee.
He said: Mr. Speaker, in my introductory remarks to begin today's second reading debate of Bill C-83, I intend to deal lightly with technical details and concentrate more on the broad objectives we will achieve through reform of legislation and regulations governing federal financial institutions.
As you are aware, Mr. Speaker, the trust and loan companies bill we are considering today is the first of several bills that, along with new regulations, will modernize the rules governing federal financial institutions.
Government Orders
Other bills will include the Bank Act, the Insurance Companies Act and the Cooperative Credit Associations Act and related statutes. All of the new statutes are to come into effect on the same date.
The government's reform will break down barriers among the pillars of the financial sector-banking, insurance and trust and loan companies-and allow financial institutions to compete more directly with each other.

The trust and loan companies bill and the subsequent bills and regulations contain four essential elements. First, they establish rules for an ownership policy that allows for both closely held and widely held institutions.
Second, they establish a new framework for competition in the financial sector through the removal of many of the remaining rules that presently restrict institutions from fully competing with each other.
Third, they update prudential safeguards to reflect the new world in which financial institutions will operate.
Fourth, they modernize old statutes by adopting rules and procedures modelled on the Canadian Business Corporations Act.

The reform, Mr. Speaker, maintains wide ownership for Schedule I banks, including the six largest Canadian banks. This ensures that no one person or group of associated persons can own more than 10 per cent of any class of bank shares. These requirements are consistent with international rules and practices about the ownership of banks.
Large trust, loan and stock insurance companies will be required to ensure that at least 35 per cent of their shares are widely held and publicly traded within five years. Significant changes in the ownership of financial institutions will be subject to approval by the Minister of Finance, who will take account of whether transfers are in the best interests of the Canadian financial system.
Although these rules may appear to be technical adjustments, or tinkering, they are significant in part because they represent adjustments to an industry that is of major importance. All Canadians will be affected by

October 30, 1990
Government Orders
these changes-and for the better. The sheer magnitude of the industry makes an impact on Canadians inevitable.
There are more than 3,000 Canadian financial institutions, with assets of some $900 billion. Canada's 25 largest financial institutions hold assets of more than $760 billion. A total of 23 of these institutions are federally incorporated 23 out of 25.
The manner in which the federally incorporated financial institutions serve the needs of Canadians will be directly affected by the legislative and regulatory reforms we have announced. I sincerely believe, Mr. Speaker, these institutions will operate more effectively and competitively, and that they will be more accessible to meet the objectives of Canadians.
We must not forget that the money handled by Canadian financial institutions funds the mortgages of Canadians, finances our automobile puchases, shelters and invests our savings, and makes available the investment needed for new or expanded industries and businesses. The success of these institutions is key to our economic success, as well as our security as savers and investors.
Because of the particular importance of financial institutions in channeling savings to finance economic growth, it is essential that they be sound, innovative, dynamic and internationally competitive.
The challenge has been to develop a regulatory approach that protects the public while it encourages, rather than inhibits, innovation and efficiency in our financial sector. Mr. Speaker, I believe that we have met that challenge.

The objectives of this reform of financial sector legislation are to enhance protection for depositors and policyholders. They are also to benefit consumers by increasing competition and the spectrum of services offered by financial institutions. It will strengthen the ability of Canadian financial institutions to compete at home and abroad. It will lay the groundwork for harmonization discussions with the provinces. This is very important.
These goals will be achieved under the new legislative framework and regulations.

Honourable Members will recognize that in order to protect consumers, the government had already tightened up prudential rules in 1987. These will now be further strengthened, including additional enhancements to the supervisory system. I know that the hon. member for Nickel Belt, who monitors these issues very closely, will be very interested in this aspect of our legislation. For example, tougher self-dealing rules will be implemented, the self-policing role of directors and auditors will be made more effective through mandated roles and responsibilities, and the Superintendent of Financial Institutions will have increased powers to require information that will enable problems to be anticipated. The Superintendent of Financial Institutions is therefore being given the kind of access he did not have before.
Consumers will find shopping for financial services more convenient and will benefit from a wider choice of financial products since banks, trust and loan companies and insurance companies will be allowed to compete more directly with each other. The interests of the consumer will continue to be protected.
For example, the new Bank Act would also include the service charge disclosure provisions now contained in Bill C-9, which is before Parliament. By opening new avenues of growth for Canada's financial institutions the new regulations will strengthen the ability of these institutions to meet the new challenges that have evolved in the global marketplace.
Financial institutions will be able to diversify by owning institutions operating in other segments of the financial services industry. For example, banks and insurance companies will be allowed to own trusts; in addition, trust and loan companies and banks will be permitted to own insurance companies.
Together, Mr. Speaker, these proposals set out a framework for fair competition that will allow all insitu-tions to participate.

However, we are all aware that there are competing interests within the financial institution community which cannot be completely reconciled. In those cases we have sought a reasonable balance. For example, banks and trust and loan companies will be restricted from offering most insurance services, and retailing of most insurance products in branches of deficit taking
October 30, 1990

institutions will be prohibited. This ensures that insurance will continue to be sold by qualified licensed insurance brokers and agents working independently of any deficit taking institution.
At the same time, however, banks and trust and loan companies will be given the power to promote goods and services, including insurance to their credit hard holders. The government has spent considerable time consulting on its proposals with financial institutions and their associations. It has integrated these views with its continuing analysis of the needs of an evolving and dynamic market, both nationally and internationally. This process has led to firm, pragmatic policy decisions that are being put forward to Parliament.

This exercise in re-regulation represents a balancing of individual, national, international, federal-provincial and commercial and prudential concerns that will, as a package, serve the public interest well and permit our financial institutions to get on with the job.
The measures set out a framework for strong national institutions that serve the national interest. The reforms also respect provincial rights of supervision and authority in the financial sector.
There is a need for greater consistency among federal and provincial rules in order to avoid balkanization of regulatory regimes and permit our institutions to compete more effectively at home and abroad.
The new legislation and proposals take into account a number of concerns that have been expressed by the provinces regarding matters such as commercial links, the in-house trust powers of banks, and provisions allowing for improved sharing of information among federal and provincial supervisors of financial institutions. This opens the door to in-depth discussions with the provinces to clarify responsibilities for the supervision of financial institutions.
Co-operation between federal and provincial authorities is the most responsible way of ensuring the stability and growth of our national and regional financial institutions. This would reduce the possibility of regulatory and supervisory duplication.
Government Orders
The goal, Mr. Speaker, is to avoid, in pratical terms and to the degree possible, the multiple regulation of federal and other institutions operating in several jurisdictions. This approach could be designed to have institutions regulated as much as possible by their jurisdiction of incorporation.

Mr. Speaker, I believe we have much work before us. I hope that I can count, and I am sure that I can, on the co-operation of the House in expediting consideration of the bill now before us as well as the other bills that are to follow.
I believe that in the interests of consumers and in support of increased competitiveness for Canada's financial institutions, it is time for us to get on with the business of reform.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to be able to speak in favour of the motion for second reading of Bill C-83 regarding financial institutions. I am pleased to do so mainly because modern legislation is urgently needed by the financial industry and we, as legislators, have a duty to help them compete in the new global market.
We also have an equally important duty to protect consumers and ensure the soundness of the financial system in Canada. I believe that all of these interests will be best served by getting this bill past second reading and into committee. Once in committee, we intend to conduct a very thorough study of the legislation.
The need for financial sector reform has become so urgent because this government has been incredibly slow in responding to the needs of the industry with new modem legislation.
The Conference Board of Canada refers to the: "repeated delays in financial sector reform and the urgency for policy makers to move ahead with new legislation in this area". It is in this spirit that we will be supporting this motion.
When the Minister of State for Finance last month tabled this trust and loan company bill and released the policy paper concerning banks and insurance companies, we in the opposition and those in industry, were extremely pleased because this government had finally decided to act. We were disappointed, however, that the government only introduced a policy paper on banks, not

October 30, 1990
Government Orders
a new Bank Act. We were disappointed for two reasons. One, without a new Bank Act, the government's picture of financial system reform remains incomplete. Two, the current act expires in five months, and when the act expires banks lose their licences.
Last week, the minister did introduce a last-minute bill that would extend the current Bank Act one year until April, 1992. This will prevent the chartered banks from losing their licences, but this last minute piecemeal approach has been typical of the way this government has been handling financial reform and many other matters.
The government's policy process started about five and a half years ago. First there was the green paper in April 1985, followed a year and a half later by a blue paper in December 1986. That was followed by promise after promise after promise by this government that new legislation was coming soon. The industry waited and waited and waited. Soon, it turned out, meant not in six months, or even in 12, soon turned into four years, during which the Canadian financial industry watched their global market share tumble.
For example, look at the Royal Bank, Canada's largest. According to the Economic Council of Canada, the Royal Bank ranked sixteenth in the world in terms of assets in 1981. Today, it is around 57th. In nine years the Royal Bank went from being 16th down to 57th. Consider the fact that during the early 1980s we had four banks in the top 50. Now we have none. Even countries much smaller than Canada, such as Switzerland, Hong Kong, and the Netherlands boast larger institutions than our own.
Look at international loans. Canadian financial institutions make only 3 per cent of the world's international loans versus almost 8 per cent seven years ago. That is a tremendous decrease in the last eight years.
Any way you look at it, Canada's financial institutions are facing fierce global competition. It is a war out there, but this present government, has been allowing our banks and other financial institutions to go out and to compete with one hand tied behind their back.
That is why I am very pleased to welcome this legislation concerning trust and loan companies which we are debating today. There are several reasons why this new financial legislation is needed in Canada. I spoke briefly about the first one, globalization. The others include the Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement, Europe 1992, and provincial deregulation.
First, globalization. Financial institutions have undergone massive transformation in recent years. As technology has advanced, geographical barriers have retreated, turning several international markets into one huge global market. Billions of dollars can be sent around the globe in a matter of seconds, 24 hours a day.
The globalization of financial markets has been driven by the needs of both borrowers and investors. For corporate and government borrowers alike, the search for the cheapest source of funds has known no national boundaries. Like individual Canadian consumers, those corporations and governments are price-shy and they go where the money is the cheapest.
For large portfolio managers and other investors, the incentive has been better investment opportunities and greater diversification of portfolios.
Canadian financial institutions are well aware of the potential advantages in this new global marketplace. In fact, Canadian Bankers Association president, Helen Sinclair says Canadian banks have "made a virtual obsession of the question of their role in the global marketplace".
Another major issue highlighting the need for financial reform is the Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement. The FTA changed the rules concerning financial institutions in two major ways. One, American banks entering Canada have had the limits on their asset growth removed and they can now open new branches without permission from the government. Two, Americans can now buy up to 100 per cent of any Canadian financial institution, whereas before they were limited to buying a total of 25 per cent.
Also related to the free trade agreement is American Express. It received government approval to operate as a bank in Canada, even though the company is not regulated as a bank in the United States, which is an apparent contradiction of Canadian law. It is not a contradiction of this government's policies because if

Canadian financial institutions understandably felt that the playing field had been shifted in favour of the Americans. This was because the new AMEX Bank was owned by commercial enterprise, a type of ownership forbidden to Canadian banks. Clearly the issue of the level playing field in Canada is one that this reform package must resolve.
The free trade agreement also established the ground rules for another round of international negotiations, those surrounding Europe 1992. As the European Community moves towards a 12-country, 320 million person market, Canada must be involved. But in order to gain permission for its financial institutions to operate in that market, Canada will be under great pressure to grant to the Europeans the same privileges granted to the Americans under the free trade agreement, especially the exemption from the asset ceiling on Schedule 2 banks.
The second issue arising from Europe 1992 is the inability of Canada's federal government and the 10 provinces to achieve harmonization in financial institutions, compared to the 12 countries in Europe. Clearly, then, the government's new financial package must address federal-provincial harmonization.
In fact, the lack of Canadian harmonization is another force, a major force, pushing the need for reform. Several provinces, including Quebec, Ontario, New Brunswick, and British Columbia, have updated their legislation regarding financial institutions considerably over the past few years. While the federal government has been operating at a standstill, the provinces have been moving ahead.
The most far-reaching changes are taking place in Quebec which in 1987 introduced its blueprint for financial sector reform. These changes included the blurring of the four so-called pillars: the banks, the trust and loan companies, insurance companies, and securities dealers. They also included the acceptance of financial and commercial links, where commercial enterprise, such as a steel company, could own a financial institution such as a trust company or credit union.

I would like to address some of the major issues that have been raised by the government's reform package. These are issues that certainly must be resolved before meaningful reform of Canada's financial institutions can take place. I will deal with them under four separate headings: powers, ownership, regulation, and supervision.
The situation before this reform package came along is that trust and loan companies can, among other things, take consumer and commercial deposits and are involved in the mortgage business. They do not have full commercial or consumer lending powers yet. However, Bill C-83 will change that.
The first issue under the heading of powers is networking, or the ability of a financial institution from one pillar to offer its network offices to promote or to sell the products of an institution from another pillar.
As we know, Bill C-83 gives trust and loan companies natural personal powers or, in other words, allows them to engage in whatever financial activity is not expressly forbidden by law. The present trust and loan companies can do only what the law expressly permits them to do.
This kind of opening up of the financial services industry in principle is a good thing because it gives consumers more choice and it should ensure more competition. However, I wonder if the government knows what it is doing by throwing the market wide open in this way. What are the costs? What are the benefits associated with this new openness? Other issues under the powers heading include the question of whether financial institutions should be able to promote goods and services, including insurance, to their credit card holders and the whole question of allowing banks into the auto leasing business.

Under the ownership heading are issues such as closely versus widely-held ownership of financial institu-

tions, commercial financial links, banks owning insurance companies, and the question of foreign ownership.
The ownership situation now is that trust companies can be closely held and can have commercial links. There are institutions such as Canada Trust, which has one major shareholder, Imasco, which owns a drugstore company, a tobacco company, and other commercial ventures. Many insurance companies are closely held, have commercial links, although some, mainly life insurance companies, are widely held and do not have commercial links.
Banks, on the other hand, cannot have commercial links and must be widely held, meaning that no one can own more than 10 per cent.
The issue of closely versus widely-held ownership is crucial because it deals with soundness of the financial system in Canada. A case can be made for either side, and I want to summarize very briefly both of those.
First, the broad ownership of financial institutions has come to be recognized by some as a very effective way of protecting the misuse of depositors' funds and self-dealing which might occur if there was just one major shareholder.
Second, widely held ownership is seen as preventing discrimination by a financial institution against potential borrowers who happen to be competitors of the institution's major shareholder.
There is also a case for closely held ownership. The first argument is that, while the stated goals of widely held ownership are admirable, the cost to the trust industry, for example, might be just too high.
They argue that if you are concerned about self-dealing and other abuses, there are better ways to guard against them than imposing strict ownership limits. They point to better regulation, bans on self-dealing and rules to expose conflicts of interest. This is the way to prevent these abuses, they argue, not imposing one ownership structure on all financial institutions simply because it sounds good in theory.
Turning now to the specific question of commercial-financial links, again we see strong arguments for and against. Those in favour of these links say a commercial parent would be able to increase the capital of the financial institutions, which is very important in such a competitive industry.

Some say that the existence of a strong shareholder would also provide an opportunity to make the management of the financial institution more responsive to the wishes of its shareholders and less likely to grow stagnant.
Commercial links, according to this side, would also allow the parent institution to diversify its sources of revenue, thus contributing to the overall income stability of the group.

Both would be able to operate more efficiently and compete effectively with the large conglomerates from Japan and Europe.
Indeed, one argument for commercial-financial links is that Canada may have no choice but to allow them, given the growth of such links around the world, and even within Canada. Denying federally-chartered financial institutions access to such links, the argument goes, would be asking them to compete with one arm behind their back.
Finally, those in favour of commercial-financial links point to the case of the American Express Bank which has commercial links and is competing against Canadian banks which are denied access to such links. The opponents of financial-commercial links counter that these links may lead to self-dealing, conflict of interest situations. Even for a financial institution that is otherwise well run, just the appearance of commercial interference could reduce depositor confidence in the institution.
They also argue that, just as a commercial parent could improve the balance sheet of the financial institution, just the opposite could very well happen and one would see an unhealthy commercial parent threatening the

Another major ownership issue relates to foreign ownership of Canadian financial institutions. Canadian financial markets are relatively open. Allowing foreign institutions access to our domestic market has served to increase the competitiveness of the Canadian financial system generally, to the benefit of consumers. It has also allowed Canadian institutions the right to operate in other countries, thereby strengthening their operations back home.
Currently, foreigners can open financial institutions in all four pillars and may own 100 per cent of those institutions they create. They may also buy into existing institutions, but individuals cannot own more than 10 per cent of banks, while trust companies and insurance firms, and total non-U.S. foreign ownership cannot exceed 25 per cent. No restrictions apply to individuals or total foreign ownership of securities dealers.
Under the free trade agreement, however, Americans are exempted from these rules and generally have the same ownership rights as Canadians, in terms of federally-chartered financial institutions. Provincially-char-tered trust, insurance and securities dealers are not affected by the free trade agreement.
A major objective of any financial reform package, therefore, must be to encourage Canadian ownership of our financial institutions. We need strong Canadian financial institutions so they can look after Canadian interests first.
Turning very briefly to the areas of regulation and supervision, the primary concern is ensuring the solvency of our financial institutions. Threats to solvency come in various forms, such as self-dealing, where a bank, for example, makes a questionable loan to one of its directors.
Solvency could also be threatened by a conflict of interest. For example, where a trust company makes a questionable loan to a company affiliated with its parent
company.
There are now many rules in place to prevent such abuses, and Bill C-83 expands those rules. The question, however, is whether these rules go far enough to protect the solvency of our financial institutions, or whether they go so far that harmless, everyday transactions get hampered. This is an area that we will be examining closely in the legislative committee.
Finally, looking quickly at supervision, we see in the government's reform plan an enhanced role for the Superintendent of Financial Institutions in terms of federally chartered institutions. While I welcome that move by the government, I must remind it of the need for better harmonization of federal laws with the provinces, and I repeat my request that the Minister of State for Finance accept the invitation of the provinces to join their conference of ministers responsible for financial institutions so that there can be a meaningful dialogue between Ottawa and the provinces.

Mr. Speaker, one of the most important aspects of Canadian culture is amateur sport. Canadian college football's Vanier Cup, named after a former Governor General, is one of the few truly national sporting events. It is a Canadian event played between Canadian teams by Canadian athletes.
CBC radio has broadcast almost all the Vanier Cups live since the first game in November, 1965. However, CBC radio's program director in Toronto has apparently decided that this year's November 24 game at the SkyDome will not be broadcast because, as she puts it, sport in general and the Vanier Cup in particular have limited cultural and historical significance.
Canadians from sea to sea want to listen to the Vanier Cup on CBC radio. I would encourage CBC radio to reconsider its decision and broadcast the 1990 Vanier Cup.

Mr. Speaker, nearly 70,000 newborns have been tested for AIDS without the knowledge or consent of their parents. Worse yet, the parents of the 21 babies, and 6 are from the Ottawa area, who were subsequently found to have the HIV antibodies were not informed, nor has a record been kept of the names of the infants. This is a terrible abuse of the rights of parents.
The University of Toronto, with funding from the Department of National Health and Welfare, has been carrying out these tests. Although its procedures may be legal, I have to seriously question the ethics.
Research into AIDS is vital. The minister must look into methods, which are acceptable to the general public, of conducting necessary studies, but also that tests be documented to enable parents and doctors the proper mechanism of tracing the possible transmitter of the virus.

Mr. Speaker, today, the tenth and final report of our Auditor General, Kenneth Dye, is tabled. In those 10 years he has served his office well and the people of Canada even better.
In his report today he says, "I came to Ottawa because I had been intrigued by my predecessor's innovative ideas about comprehensive auditing. I also like constructive change and thought I could contribute to the advancement of accountability, perhaps implanting the

October 30, 1990
notion that public servants should spend people's money as carefully as they would their own."
He has pursued these ideals relentlessly through his 10 years and can retire from his job content in the knowledge that, although there is much work yet to be done, he has successfully focused government attention on efficient and effective use of public funds.
The New Democratic caucus wants to extend our thanks to Mr. Dye for his hard work over his 10 years as Auditor General and wish him much success in his transition back to private life.

Mr. Speaker, Canada Career Week is not just an opportunity for youth to learn about the career opportunities available to them, but it is also an opportunity for all of us and for adults everywhere to look at the contributions we can make toward encouraging our youth to complete their training.
The most important thing we can do is change our attitudes toward skills training and non-academic education. We must realize that a student who does not excel in English literature is not less intelligent than the student who does. They have different aptitudes but both are equally important to our communities and both deserve the same amount of encouragement and respect.
Through education, we give our youth self-reliance and an opportunity to be productive adults. By encouraging our youth to be the best they can be-bricklayer, welder, teacher, scientist, or whatever-we instil self-respect and self-confidence which, in turn, promotes a healthy regard for the achievement of others. Investing in skills training is an investment that keeps on giving us a return. I cannot think of another investment with such guarantees.

Mr. Speaker, yesterday, the President of the Treasury Board
tabled a report on the use of the federal government's six Challenger jets. Incredible but true, Mr. Speaker: there has been a 40-per cent drop since the Conservative Government was elected in 1984.
Under the Liberal government, which means until August 1984, the Liberals took 672 flights in twelve months. In two twelve-month periods, in 1989 and 1990, the Conservative Government used the Challenger jets 258 and 301 times, respectively.
Mr. Speaker, this is one more example of good management by this government.

Mr. Speaker, my constituents of Hamilton Mountain, as well as most other Canadians, are worried about the effect the proposed GST will have on their standard of living. I would like to point out to Canadians yet another flaw in the government's proposed new tax.
Close scrutiny of the GST shows that not all Canadians will be treated equally under this new tax. For example, stockbrokers' fees will be GST exempt. Commissions charged by other professions, such as auto dealers, real estate agents, and art brokers, are all taxable. Yet the commissions charged by stockbrokers are exempt. Is it not interesting that the Minister of Finance cannot find a way to tax his former colleagues and employers?
When a government introduces a piece of legislation that will hit the poor and the elderly the hardest and gives the boys on Bay Street a break, it should come as no surprise that the Liberal caucus, under Jean Chretien, would vow to scrap such a tax.

Mr. Speaker, while the government has pushed interest rates to the 14 per cent mark, it is ignoring the hardships it has imposed on Canadians.
Housing starts are at their lowest level in six years. Home sales have plunged 30 per cent compared to last year and the construction industry is expected to have an unemployment rate of 15 per cent.
Across the country, families earning $40,000 or $50,000 a year are defaulting on their mortgages, a jump of 41 per cent in the last six months. In Toronto hundreds of homeowners have already had to give up their properties and default on their dream homes.
While the Tories stick to their destructive high interest rate policy, CMHC has predicted a continued rise in defaults in the coming year. The Canadian Real Estate Association, meeting here in Ottawa today, is under no illusion as to what the problem is. It is interest rates.
As the unemployment rate increases and interest rates push housing prices higher and higher, hundreds of thousands of Canadians are shoved out of the market to buy their first home.
This is the price Canadians are paying for the government's inflation-fighting tactics. The long-term damage to the Canadian economy is a price not worth paying.

October 30,1990
Mr. Speaker, here we go again. We have heard it all before. Jean Chretien and the Liberal Party are telling Canadians they will scrap the GST if elected.
That will never happen.
Hear, hear.

But can we really believe them? Not if you look at Liberal history, Mr. Speaker.
Remember the 1974 election? The Liberals promised us no wage and price controls. What happened less than one year into their term? We had price and wage controls.
Then, in 1980 the Liberal Party forced an election over a proposed 18-cent per gallon gasoline tax, and what happened? By the time they were turfed from office in 1984 gas prices had risen by 99 cents per gallon.
Shame.
This latest announcement is another signal to Canadians of the Liberal Party's cynical approach to government. And yes, Mr. Speaker, we have heard it all before.
Hear, hear.

Mr. Speaker, I rise today to bring to the attention of the House a scandalous example of program abuse and ineptitude by officials of ACOA and, indeed, perhaps the minister responsible.
I refer of course to the circumstances surrounding the approval of a $12 million loan to a company owned by Rick Black, NSC Diesel Inc.
Even before the building was finished, the company's orders dried up and its business plan was found to be total fabrication. The result is dozens of contractors who extended lines of credit now facing bankruptcy themselves, hundreds of their employees losing their jobs, and more economic misery for the people of this part of Nova Scotia because of this fiasco.
Now that the federal Auditor General, in response to my request to review this smelly deal, has concluded that program assessment criteria were not followed, it is time for a full public disclosure on how this deal got funded, who was zooming who, and for heads to roll, starting with the minister responsible.

Mr. Speaker, imagine, if you will, being on the receiving end of a call from a four-year old child who wants to know how to commit suicide. Imagine the pain in that child's life.
Twenty-five thousand children a month make calls for help to the Kids Help Line. On Monday, two of their phone lines will be closed. Based on last year's statistics, this means that over the next six months 100,000 kids will not be responded to by the hot-line, 2,000 suicidal kids will not receive counselling, and 9,000 kids who are the victims of family violence will not have access to a counsellor.
This service has proved itself invaluable in direct intervention and now has over 300,000 pieces of data on the nature of the difficulties faced by children in Canada. Surely the new minister responsible for children will not let this proven program deteriorate when the need is so great. Could the $72,000 the government used promoting the children's summit have been better spent?

Does he have any idea how he is going to change the tax system? Is it going to be from consumption tax? Is it going to be personal income tax?

Mr. Speaker, first of all I simply will not accept the allegation of the hon. member that we are moving ahead cynically with cases from the Caribbean as opposed to other kinds of cases. That is simply not a fact.
October 30,1990

Second, I would like to thank the Auditor General for some of his suggestions. As indicated in his report, we were moving on many of the areas that he made suggestions on-both in the backlog and in the new system, and in our over-all immigration plan leading to our five-year levels-because we understood as well that there were some problems in our management.
Since the end of March things have changed; 50 per cent of the cases within the backlog have now been opened because we have improved our processes, and 30 per cent of them have been decided.
The Auditor General also suggested that we should use greater deterrents. Perhaps that is what the critic for the NDP is suggesting.

Mr. Speaker, the Auditor General has also confirmed that the government's new refugee determination system is falling behind, taking nine months instead of nine weeks to process people and resolve their refugee claims. And the refugee board's own figures show a new backlog in a year and a half of something like 25,000 unresolved cases.
When will the minister admit that the new system also is failing and bring in the quick and fair system that was asked for several years ago by the churches and other public groups in Canada?

speakeroldname: Hon. Barbara McDougall (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, as I recall, when we brought in our new system, the part of the new system that the hon. member was most against was the safe third country provision. Is he now suggesting that in the interest of speed we bring that in?

Mr. Speaker, my question is addressed to the minister of housing. In large urban centres such as Toronto and Vancouver the average family still cannot afford to purchase the average home. The problem is that first-time home buyers in Toronto need a down payment of up to $60,000.
Will the minister consider changing the rules so that people with funds in RRSPs can use that money for down payments, or will the government make it possible for first-time home buyers to set up self-directed RRSPs
Oral Questions
to be used for those down payments, thereby making home ownership more affordable.

Mr. Speaker, the suggestion put forward by the hon. member is one of a number of suggestions that are going to be discussed tomorrow and the next day at the Canadian Housing Finance Conference which, as you know, Mr. Speaker, is the first ever housing financing conference held in this country. It will bring together 150 experts from Canada and internationally, from business, from the financial community, academics, to focus on what can be done to make housing more affordable, and to allow more accessibility to home ownership.
The Department of Finance had some understandable concerns with respect to the use of RRSPs for housing down payments. They obviously do not want to raise the expectations of Canadians that something of that sort will be brought in immediately, but at the same time, it is something that is under careful examination at the present time.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Transport. As Minister of Transport, I am sure he is aware that there is only one highway into Nova Scotia and on to Newfoundland.
Elimination of rail freight in Newfoundland has resulted in dramatic increases in truck traffic on this highway. Since being elected less than two years ago I have witnessed several accidents on this highway, resulting in fatalities to men, women, and children. Last Friday night was the most recent but sadly I know there will be more. We desperately need a new federal-provincial agreement to stop the fatalities and the grief.
Will the minister negotiate, with all the urgency required, a new co-operation agreement to have this overburdened highway replaced?

Mr. Speaker, I presume my hon. friend realizes and appreciates that highways are a provincial responsibility. However, I would say that my provincial colleagues and I recently approved phase four of the national highway system study at the recent Council of Transport Ministers

October 30, 1990
Oral Questions
meeting and we are looking at the priorities at the present time.
But I should also tell him that there has been no decision made on funding mechanisms at this time.

Mr. Speaker, I thank the hon. member for his patience. I want to follow the President of the Treasury Board in making a few comments about the Auditor General.
Today the Auditor General tabled his last report in the House after serving this Parliament for 10 years. It is a big job for a person to come in and take over because

October 30, 1990
Point of Order
government is big business. It cannot possibly be done all in one year. It has to be divided up in cycles, with parts done parts each year. Even in that time, it is a big job.
I think the Auditor General has some very fine achievements to his record, as indicated by the President of the Treasury Board, achieving that certain reservations no longer exist. For example, today Public Service pension funds that are owed by the government as part of the debt of the government and also the foreign loans that will not probably be collected are now part of the country's liabilities.

As Chairman of the Public Accounts Committee I can say that the Auditor General and his staff have been most co-operative. In the years ahead, it is going to be very important that we have a good successor to the present Auditor General who has laid so much very important ground work. The taxpayers of this country and probably any free country of the world are going to demand greater accountability of their parliaments and their legislatures and, indeed, they are going to ask for greater accountability from their individual members of Parliament and representatives. I think that is one thing that we all have to accept as part of democracy.
The Auditor General has been very adamant in his protection of the public purse. It is very important that this Parliament support the Auditor General, his office, and his staff. It is very important that the public accounts committee co-operate and work very closely with him. Of course, it is very important that he has the support of the people of Canada because he is the one that is going to protect their purse.
Many countries send their auditors general to Canada to learn our system. That simply indicates the good programs put together with approximately 690 personnel in the Auditor General's office and a system whereby other people who are experts a in the field, perhaps
atomic energy or defence matters, can be brought in on short-term contracts, and then let go.
He has put together a very good program. He has been an outstanding servant to the country. I hope that those who are searching for a new Auditor General for the next 10 years will indeed find the qualities in the new man that have existed in Kenneth Dye.
Hear, hear.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to join with the other two members who have spoken of the Auditor General and the work that he has done, on behalf of my party, the New Democratic Party.

Mr. Speaker, we in this party unanimously agree that in fact he has done his best and he has done an excellent job for the people of Canada. Thank you, Auditor General.

speakeroldname: Mr. Dave Worthy (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of State (Privatization and Regulatory Affairs) and Minister of State (Finance)):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Finance); Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Privatization and Regulatory Affairs)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is my pleasure to rise and speak to the trust and loans bill. My
first comment has to be that the trust and loans bill does not stand alone. It fits into the total reform package of bills and will encompass all of our financial institutions in Canada.
I will be trying to explain briefly some of the history we have gone through in arriving at this bill and how the bill has taken into consideration the various needs of the institutions, the consumers and the people in Canada.
The historical framework within which Bill C-83 is being brought forward is a process of reform of the financial sector, and is not a quick one. The process in fact has been said by many people to have taken too long. However, I think hon. members will agree that it is wise to deliberate longer and to make sure that what we do come up with is workable.
In this bill the minister and his staff have been pragmatic and practical and propose what in large part has taken years of consultation and consideration to arrive at.
At the beginning of its mandate, the government recognized the need for reform. Therefore, in April 1985, it brought forward the green paper. This green paper resulted in many discussions across Canada. Committee reports were made on it, and as a result of these discussions, as well as input from the industry and the public, the proposals underwent refinement. This led to the tabling in December 1986 of the paper entitled New Directions for the Financial Sector. Once again, there were further discussions, draft legislation was compiled at this point and the trust and loans companies draft legislation was tabled for discussion purposes in December 1987. Of course, further consultation took place subsequent to that.
Throughout this period, as well, several other pieces of legislation did come into effect to make temporary improvements to the system. These were Bills C-42 and C-56. These bills implemented a number of changes in the regime governing the financial institutions, particularly with respect to the supervisory functions now exercised by the Superintendent of Financial Institutions. These, in effect, created a stronger position for the Superintendent, and this has been recognized by all parties and throughout the industry as being a very positive move.
October 30, 1990

The government has been active in pursuing the reform of the financial sector. We have also been careful to ensure that our proposals will be effective as well as practical. We know that there is no point in producing reforms that look good but in the final analysis will not work.
I believe that the measures recommended in Bill C-83 will be found to be effective as well as practical. Because they will be practical, they may fall short of some of the aspirations of many of the parties. Because they are broadly acceptable to all sectors of the industry, there will no doubt be some people who wish that one provision or another were a little different. This is the case, however, where it would be impossible to grant everyone's wishes fully. There are too many legitimately different points of view. The government has settled on proposals which meet the needs of the economy and the institution, as well as the Canadian public.
It is important to remember that with the size and importance of this sector, there are four sets of needs which this legislation must recognize and fulfil.
First, there are the needs of the economy. The financial system is not just an important segment of the economy in terms of its size, it is a vital support system without which the economy as a whole would grind to a halt. The easiest and fastest way to harm the economy is to have a financial system that does not meet the current needs of companies and individuals. Conversely, a healthy and dynamic financial system will strengthen the whole economy. Anyone who has bought a car, has tried to get a mortgage on a house, has tried to finance their business, knows that the financial institutions in this country play a critical role in our economy.
There are also the needs of the institutions themselves. The trust and loans legislation was enacted in the first 20 years of this century. If my memory serves me correctly, it was 1917. It is in excess of 70 years since this legislation was first enacted and obviously there have been many changes in the environment in which they operate, many changes to their needs and, of course, this legislation must take that into account.
Then, of course, there are the needs of the consumers and the public. They need information and assurance that the health of the institution with which they are
Government Orders
dealing are honourable and that they can have confidence in dealing with them.
They also require the improved services that the financial institutions in Canada want to provide for them and, of course, it is up to us to make sure that this legislation does provide this increased responsiveness to the Canadian public.
In addition, there is another important demand placed on these proposals and that is the need to harmonize with the provincial governments. If a person is going to create a viable financial business in British Columbia or in Quebec, or one that is going to function across the country, it is obvious that the regulations controlling these institutions have to be co-ordinated.
It is recognized by the Department of Finance and our minister in producing this bill that harmonization with the province and their regulations must take place. The co-operation between the two levels of government is the most responsible way of ensuring that the health of all Canadian financial institutions is maintained. I am pleased to say that the proposals for reform are substantially met in the bill that we are tabling.
I would like to get into a few of the points of the bill itself, how it addresses the needs of these various people in the tax reform. I want to reiterate first, though, the important point that the principles of this bill are not isolated. They are part of the larger reform process and must be discussed in the context of that larger reform. All four pillars of our financial institutions are being addressed and the bill today, of course, just addresses the trust and loans, but it must work in harmony with the other bills to follow.
The bill will achieve four things. Initially, it will revitalize the rules of ownership. They will allow for both closely-held and widely-held institutions. It is required that it revitalize the framework for competition in the financial sector. This will be done by removing many of the restrictions imposed now on financial institutions so that they can compete fully with each other.
There has to be, of course, updates to the prudential safeguards. These will be providing protection for the depositors as well as the policy holders. In the process of this, we will be, as a by-product, modernizing the existing statutes.

October 30, 1990
Government Orders
Let us look first and quickly at the framework for competition. The general policy of the government with respect to competition is that consumers and institutions should be able to have the opportunity to offer similar ranges of service and competing markets previously not open to them. This is intended to enhance the choices available to our consumers.
We propose that with appropriate approval and subject to some relatively minor restrictions, financial institutions will be able to diversify into new financial businesses through their subsidiaries. This follows on the provisions of legislation passed in 1987 which permitted federally chartered financial institutions to own security dealers.
Under the new provisions, trust companies may be owned by institutions without trust powers, such as banks and insurance companies, and trust companies may themselves now own insurance companies. Similar provisions will apply to other types of financial institutions not covered by this bill before us today.
In considering whether to approve the purchase of a financial institution by another in a similar business, the minister will, of course, take into account the size of the buyer and the size of the institution being acquired.
Trust and loan companies will also receive full consumer lending powers. Full commercial lending powers will also be available to them, as long as they satisfy the conditions which will ensure that they have the necessary staff and controls in place to manage the commercial portfolio. Banks, of course, as an ancillary to this, will be able to offer portfolio management and investment advice services, inhouse.
Trust and loan companies will also be allowed to network financial services offered by affiliates or independent financial institutions, subject to the restrictions on retailing of insurance.
I would like to get into that, just briefly, because there are some things that deposit takers are not going to be permitted to do and it is important that we, as legislators, and that all Canadians should be aware of them. First, with a few limited exceptions, banks and trust and loan companies will not be allowed to retail insurance or to distribute insurance applications through their branches. The exceptions are credit-related life insurance and
travel insurance, which they have provided for many years.
Second, while a deposit-taking institution may own an insurance company, the operations of the two businesses have to be kept separate. It is important to recognize that this approach carefully balances several policy objectives. It promotes a degree of extra competition that we believe will be healthy and beneficial for consumers but without disrupting the long-established business of insurance retailers. Licensed brokers and agents will continue to be able to give their clients professional advice on which insurance companies and policies will best serve their needs.
Also, no financial institution will be able to engage in car leasing and this is something for which there has been a lot of demand for by financial institutions and about which a great deal of concern in the general marketplace.
In theory, the idea of financial institutions being in the car leasing business is very attractive but it flounders at one critical point. Banks are already extensively engaged in the business of financing car dealers and they also are in the business of providing consumer auto loans. If, on top of this, banks were to go into the car-leasing business, there would inevitably be questions of conflict of interest. Of course, it is for this reason that the government has decided not to allow car leasing within financial institutions.
There are going to be significant changes in the ability and control of ownership within financial institutions. The government has adopted a pragmatic approach to the question of ownership. There is an area where many options have been expressed, many mutually exclusive. But I believe the proposals in the policy contained in Bill C-83 will meet the needs of all those involved.
The first step in our ownership is to ensure that the Minister of Finance has the authority to approve significant changes in ownership of federal financial institutions, as well as the existing authority to approve all start-ups. This is an increased responsibility for the minister and, of course, the opportunity for increased flexibility within the system. Specifically, an investor will be required to obtain the minister's approval of any purchase of shares which will result in ownership of more than 10 per cent of any class of shares held in that company. Investors now owning more than 10 per cent of the shares of an institution will be required to gain
October 30,1990

approval from the minister for the purchase of additional shares.
Finally, an investor must gain approval to acquire control of a company that is linked to a financial institution, when the result is a change in the significant ownership interest of that institution.
Trust and loan companies will continue to be able to be closely held and, in fact, they will be able to be sold on closely held basis. But if a trust and loan company is of any significant size, in fact, if it has assets in excess of $750 million or more, it will be required to take the necessary steps to ensure that at least 35 per cent of the total voting rights attached to the shares are widely held and listed for public trading on a Canadian stock exchange. Institutions will have five years to comply with this provision, which is very fair. A Canadian financial holding company or a Canadian-regulated financial institution could be able to meet the rule on behalf of its trust, loan, or insurance company subsidiary.
I would like to mention now the credential safeguards. These are the safeguards put in place in the legislation for the depositors and policyholders. A major focus of concern in the financial sector, as in business generally, is what is known as self-dealing. This is of a great deal of concern to the government, and I believe it is of great concern to all members in the House.
Our proposals embodied in this bill are based on three elements: a general ban on non-arm's length transactions, internal controls and screening of permitted transactions, and a preclearance of certain special transactions by the Superintendent of Financial Institutions. Institutions will be required to set up committees of the board, one the conduct review committee, to clear these transactions that are permitted. These conduct review committees will have a majority of their members independent of the institution.
Certain improvements will be made to the existing supervisory system. Specifically, the superintendent will gain the power to demand information from owners of federal financial institutions. As well, any director who resigns as a result of disagreement with other directors or officers of the company, or any auditor resigning or being placed at the company's request will be required to
Government Orders
submit a written statement to the superintendent. Affiliated directors will now have to make up one-third of the boards of directors and, to enhance the possibility of minority shareholders being represented on the board, a system of cumulative voting will be introduced for institutions where any shareholder owns more than 10 per cent of any class of voting shares.
Finally, our policy requires federally regulated financial institutions to put into place procedures to resolve conflict of interest.
I believe this legislation is appropriate. It is the fruit of many, many years of consultation and its provisions express principles that will operate to the benefit of the financial sector, the economy, and in fact all Canadians. I am proud to be able to speak in support of this bill and I urge its consideration to the House.

It is my duty, pursuant to Standing Order 38 to inform the House that the questions to be raised tonight at the time of adjournment are as follows: the hon. member for Markham- Whitchurch-Stouffville-Gun control; the hon. member for Dartmouth-Goods and Services Thx; the hon. member for Trinity-Spadina-Immigration.

October 30,1990

On questions or comments, the hon. member for Scarborough-Agincourt.

Mr. Speaker, I listened to the hon. member with great interest. I had an opportunity in the past year to meet with a member of the board of the Bank of Nova Scotia, Mr. Gordon Bell, who is also the chairman of the bank. Mr. Bell and I had a lengthy discussion and he tried to convey to me why the bank should be allowed to sell insurance over the counter.
The question that I have to pose to the member is: Does he feel that in any way, shape or form the insurance industry will be hurt? If so, in what way, if the banks are allowed to compete? Does the hon. member not see that, if this is allowed to the banks, it would give the general public a much easier means of obtaining insurance? Also, in the sense of trade, does he not see that it will lower the insurance rates along with the charges of insurance on individuals?

I would like to thank the member from Scarborough for his question.
There has been a great deal of interest, not only by banks, which the hon. member mentioned, but also from trust institutions. Any institute that has depositors and branches has encouraged us to consider giving them the ability to be able to sell retail insurance from their branches.
As has been stated very strongly by the insurance companies, their representatives, and people concerned with the issue, the insurance companies now do a very good job of selling insurance. There is a lot of competition already. The feeling was that the professionalism shown by the industry and the ability to deal properly with it was more properly done through insurance companies.
Of course, banks will be able to have insurance companies as affiliates and will be able to get into the insurance business if that is really their intention. But it is not felt to be in the over-all interests of the public, the consumers, or the financial institution to allow the retailing of insurance at the branches.
Mr. Speaker, if I could pursue that question a little further, one of the things which strikes us about this
legislation and, in fact, the broad pattern of deregulating step by step financial institutions which is taking place, is that we are going to see a situation created in which it will be possible for banks or other financial institutions to move into other fields through the takeover of existing institutions or the establishment of new institutions.
For instance, a bank will be able to establish an insurance company. It will be able to use that insurance company to promote the sale of insurance products and services through the credit card operations at the bank. There is a great deal of new scope for banks to broaden their activities. Similarly, there is a great deal of new scope for insurance companies and trust companies to broaden their activities.
Yet, there is a line which is drawn when it comes to an insurance company which a bank might set up being able to promote through credit card mailing lists and that kind of thing. It is nevertheless prevented from seeing those insurance services directly offered to the consumers of the bank on a branch-by-branch basis.
In short, it seems that one has not established a level of increased direct service or increased direct competition at the branch level of banks, for instance, that would operate as a threat to existing insurance companies. It seems to me as I look at this that there is a major question that one can raise as to whether the government is not trying to let these major financial institutions have their cake and eat it too. They would have the possibility of expanding their operations into new financial fields, yet securing from competition and securing from the possibility of better service to consumers those institutions that might be threatened by that expansion.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Finance); Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Privatization and Regulatory Affairs)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was listening carefully to the member for Essex-Windsor. I think he has put his finger right on the critical area, as I indicated in the first few statements of my speech.
There is a veiy critical balance that was required between the liberalizing or streamlining of the financial industry and yet retaining some of the controls that we feel are in the best interests of the people of Canada.
It is in this particular area where the government tried, while encouraging the competitiveness between these financial institutes, which my hon. friend indicated is there, but retaining as a policy for the existing insurance retailers, the dealers and the professional bodies that are there to service the insurance needs of the Canadian
October 30,1990

people, that that is still going to be retained and controlled as a separate entity.
The member will find that there will be people, and in our committee meetings I am sure we will hear from people, who will talk to both sides of that issue and who will be able to explore exactly why that balanced point in fact was taken.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to ask the hon. member if he would take a moment to explain to me what will happen to those depositors and consumers as a result of the initiation of this legislation.
These are consumers who were accustomed, prior to this legislation, to two things: First, the kinds of regulations that imposed very strict guidelines on each of the pillars of the institutions which he has mentioned. Such regulation was made easy by the fact that each one of them was guided by a separate body of laws and regulations. Applying the regulations to one meant that regulations were being applied to the entire industry.
Second, what would happen to the depositors who had some security, but now, faced with new legislation, the depositors and trust and loan companies will find that the regulation and therefore the security is well blurred.
