speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Finance); Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Privatization and Regulatory Affairs)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have already taken 30 seconds, the hon. member says.
I should point out first that the depositors are going to feel more secure with this legislation. The improvements to the increased powers to the superintendent should make him feel more secure. The demand that the internal control by companies to protect those same depositors should make them feel more secure as well.
Government Orders
The guidelines existed in previous aeons it seems like. It must be remembered that these are 70 years old and long overdue for a realignment. I believe that bringing them together so that all four pillars are in fact being guided by the same principles will be a dramatic breakthrough. It will be better for the banks. It will be better for the insurance companies. It will be better for the trust and loan companies and, most important, it will be better for Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, I approach this piece of legislation with a great deal of trepidation because I think that the country has been waiting a long time for changes in the banking and financial institutions of this country. At this point in time we are not quite sure, after all this deliberation, whether or not this is the most appropriate piece of legislation.
The industry: banks, life insurance companies, trust companies, and loan companies, have been waiting for close to seven years for this legislation to be produced. There are all sorts of rumours on the Hill that this House is not going to continue, but is going to be prorogued soon. I hope that this is just not another false start for people in the industry. It is a great cost to the people dealing in the financial markets to have such insecurity attached to a piece of legislation and to see it introduced to the House at a time in which there is a great deal of doubt as to whether or not we will continue. It is unfair to those people who depend upon security and continuity in their operations.
The insecurity that has been there for the last seven years is reflected in a comment in a letter written to me by a life insurance company which is concerned about its own security. They were answering the question: Has the wait cost them anything? They responded:
The truth of the matter is that the banks have had a field day compared to insurance companies. We have been waiting over 50 years for modernization of our legislation, while the banks have enjoyed regular decennial reviews which have expanded their powers each time. No stroke of the pen will make the field level. We have a lot of catching up required before any semblance of parity exists. Our industry is in some danger from both lack of modernization and from the banks getting even greater powers, including the ownership of insurance companies.

October 30, 1990
Government Orders
This concern still stands as we face this piece of legislation. For the past seven years everyone has been waiting for the government to present its great step forward. We have had several rumoured attempts in the past by this government. Either they lost the way or lost their courage in dealing with this critical issue.
Our financial institutions control billions of dollars in assets. Whether it is their savings in a bank account, or their financial security expressed through their insurance policies, the vast majority of Canadians use our financial institutions on a day-to-day basis. They demand that we have a system they can depend on.
Yet, Mr. Speaker, at this time, we find that our institutions are facing a great deal of external pressures to change. I think it is incumbent upon members of Parliament, when we are dealing with the modernization issue, to deal with it honestly and directly because those changes are taking place, whether we like it or not.
For example, I would like to list three or four factors which are really influencing the progress, or the lack of progress, in our financial institutions. First of all, the globalization of financial markets. In recent years financial institutions have undergone a massive transformation. This transformation has included the development of new financial instruments and practices for managing risks, broadening markets and improving access to funds. The increased use of technology has facilitated this transformation and has been stimulated by it.
The underlying factor shaping the transformation of financial institutions has been the globalization of markets. There are processes now in place that can handle up to 900,000 transfers in the banking system on a daily basis.
The globalization of financial markets has been driven by both the needs of borrowers and investors. For borrowers, corporations and governments alike, the request for the cheapest source of funds and a broadening of their borrowing base has been paramount.
For savers and portfolio managers, the incentive has been better investment opportunities and greater diversification of portfolios. These considerations have also driven financial institutions to take a more global view of their operations.
Canada has been very slow to adopt its financial institutions for this new international reality. Consequently, many are playing a smaller role than might have been expected and in what would appear to be their natural niche in international markets. Globally, many of our institutions are losing out to competition.
A second change taking place that affects all of our financial institutions is the implementation of the Cana-da-U.S. Free Trade Agreement. Under this agreement, American banks have gained entry into Canada and had the limits removed on the growth of their assets. Their Canadian subsidiaries are no longer required to obtain approval of Canadian authorities before opening branches in Canada, so they enjoy the same opportunities as Canadian banks.
Another significant provision under the Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement is that which exempts U.S. Schedule II banks from the asset ceilings on the size of the foreign bank sector, thus improving the ease with which they can establish branches. Many of the banks feel aggrieved by this, as do the trust companies.
Perhaps even more important to the Canadian financial institutions is the second change taking place, and that is Europe in 1992. The evolution of the European Economic Community toward a full market integration will have tremendous impacts on the Canadian financial institutions. By the end of 1992, the 12 member countries of the community will become a single market for 320 million people within which individuals, goods, services and capital will be able to move freely as they do within their own respective nations today.
The service sector is a major part of the EC 1992 program. In this field, the banking directive is the keystone of the EC program. This will make it very, very difficult to have banks such as the ones in Canada get access to the European market. In the insurance sector, for example, the EC has made, and will make, a series of proposals to achieve a single European insurance market. The aim, as for banks, is to allow insurance companies to provide their service in the community on the basis of a single authorization.
In order to gain access to provide services in the European market, Canada will be under substantial pressure to grant to the Europeans the same privileges granted to the Americans under the free trade agreement, especially the exemption from the asset ceilings for European Schedule II banks.
October 30, 1990

A third factor affecting federal legislation is the recent provincial initiatives where the financial environment has been altered significantly since 1986 relating to the legislative programs of the various provincial governments. Several provinces, including Ontario, Quebec, British Columbia and New Brunswick, have updated their legislation as it pertains to trust and loan companies. This has generally meant that provinces are in the lead in providing new directions for financial sector evolution. The most far-reaching provincial initiative is the Quebec blueprint for financial sector reform introduced in 1987.
The above factors underline the need for reforming financial institutions in Canada. There is no question about that. The question becomes one of what sort of principles should be involved and how should we approach this? I think that the principles that are very important for us to remember in the House are the principles of competition and independence. Are we increasing competition in the marketplace, are we maintaining the independence of the institutions? In many cases, as we move into a globalization process, we could become afraid that our national institutions do not have the size to compete, we may set aside the questions of independence and competition within the Canadian marketplace for these other values.
I can assure the House that we on this side are very, very concerned that that balance be struck. That is why we look forward to seeing this piece of legislation referred to the committee and discussed in detail because we want to make sure that all parties have an opportunity to be heard.
In dealing with the question of competition many people, as individual consumers, are afraid that as these institutions grow so large that their interactions with the banks, life insurance and trust and loan companies, become so impersonal that they are not able to control that interaction, that there is information out there that makes them afraid about how they are being treated. Many of us live in a world of information and we take for granted how our information is gathered and how it is exchanged. But for many people, it comes as a great surprise to find out that they thought they were doing
Government Orders
one thing at a bank or a trust company, and find out that somebody knew something else about him as a result.
I have here a letter written by a retired executive in Winnipeg who came across the most unusual example of how banks use information. I will read part of that letter because I think it is very illustrative of the concerns of Canadians as they face these changes. It states:
My bank recently contacted me by telephone noting a large cheque had passed my account in the name of an insurance company and inquiring if the bank was satisfying all of my requirements for financial services.
Subsequently, I complained to a bank vice-president citing what I felt was a misuse of confidential information and unethical practice in using a record of banking transactions, unavailable to other financial institutions, to market the bank's own financial service. I was informed that a breach of confidence would only occur if the information was shared outside of the bank and the ethical question was a fine line in a very competitive world.
Nothing is more unnerving to a businessman whose business might be vulnerable in a time of recession, or to a family that might be paying a large mortgage, to feel that a banking institution knows its every move and has every piece of information. Part of the squeeze play that can be put on a consumer is the squeeze play of using that information to the disadvantage of the consumer whether he or she be a business person or a person running a family.
The House has to be conscious of our responsibility to ensure that as we move toward the modernization of the process, which we support in every way, we do not forsake or move away from the principle of competition among these institutions. For example, we welcome the decision of the government not to allow the banks to sell insurance because we think that it sets up a retail network that would be very hard for independent people to survive. The insurance industry itself is very concerned about this. I am sure it will welcome the legislation in that context.
However, the other part of the legislation contradicts that intention when the government says that it will allow the banking industry to become involved as owners of an insurance company. If we accept that part of the principle of modernization and every other field has been integration, the very fact that we are setting up a process which allows at an ownership level an integration

October 30, 1990
Government Orders
of function, one would have to be pretty naive to assume that at the retail there would not be some products which reflect the integration.
The government has appeared to close the door on this issue, but I am wondering if it slammed it shut. Will we not see continuous pressure from the different associations which have something at stake here? We all know they are very active. Will they not come back to the government after this piece of legislation is passed and say: "We are all in this together. We have companies that do both businesses. We do not understand the rationale of why we cannot be involved in the leasing industry or in insurance selling"? Will it not just be a matter of time before we find another proposal on the table going back to the question of selling insurance?
Before this government came to power there was a different attitude to what changes would be necessary to ensure the solidity and security of our financial system. We wanted strong conflict of interest provisions and self-dealing rules. We wanted to guarantee the solvency of the players. The expansion of corporate powers into different areas of financial services was a secondary consideration, but the attitude has changed. Instead of protection for the consumer in the industry, the focus of this new legislation is exactly the opposite. It is expansion of concentration.
We have already seen what deregulation has done in other industries of national importance. For our airlines, deregulation has meant a reduction in the number of airlines and airline jobs, reductions in service for small centres, and over-all financial difficulties for the remaining carriers. The same could happen in the financial sector.
With the recent change-over to the fall schedule, I am sure all politicians from different regions in the House would join me in recognizing the fact that cities outside the Ontario-Quebec golden triangle are suffering greatly from the cutbacks in the airline industry. The reality that Canadians have to face is that the quality of the service being provided to many communities is nowhere what it was a few years ago.
Yet the basis of the argument for change is similar to the arguments that we face right here in the financial legislation: the arguments of globalization, free trade,
and changes in the national economy. Those arguments we deal with here are the same technical arguments that we dealt with under airlines deregulation. We walked away from the principles of independence and the principles of competition in airline deregulation, and we have been badly hurt by it.
Will we even have two airlines in the 1990s? Can we imagine somebody raising that question in the House a decade ago, saying that we would only have one airline in Canada? That member would not have been respected or listened to for one minute. However, right now this government, because of its commitment to free markets, cannot protect two airlines. We will be left with only one. The government does not have any appreciation of what it means in the regions and of the lack of services.
Similarly, if the government does not apply the same principles in this legislation, companies trying to survive in regional markets, companies which have developed a segment or a focus in the marketplace will not be able to withstand the pressures from the big actors to take them over. They will not be able to recapitalize. They will not be able to take on the international markets because the rules within Canada will not be able to sustain their activities.
There are several companies which need the protection of the national government. That is why we have a national government, although it is not believed on the other side of the House. We have a national government to protect the public interest in Canada. While we respond to these international conditions and set up companies so they can compete internationally, we have to remember that our purpose is to make sure the consumer of Canada is dealing with companies which are both independent and able to survive, whether they are located in Vancouver, Winnipeg, or Halifax and that unlike the chartered banks they will have a regional focus in their activities.
There are many other issues to be raised but, if we take a look at some of these factors, we have reason to think that as we go through the consideration of this legislation, as we review the powers of the financial institutions, as we deal with the issues of closely held versus widely held ownership, commercial and financial linkages, foreign ownership and the regulations dealing with financial institutions such as self-dealing and sol-
October 30, 1990

vency, we will find that it is a step in the right direction to have a piece of legislation in front of the House finally.
I must encourage the government to spend a considerable amount of time in front of the committee, to encourage witnesses to appear and to take these deliberations seriously. The purpose of the government is not to accommodate the financial institutions but to establish public interest. What is lacking in this proposed legislation is the clear establishment of public interest in favour of independents and competition.

Mr. Speaker, I have a concern about the comments the member for Winnipeg North Centre expressed. First, on Air Canada and Canadian Airlines, I am not sure they would appreciate the obituary the member opposite just gave to one of them, suggesting that one of them was going to be gone soon. I for one would have to disagree with that, but I will leave that up to the airlines to decide particularly.
The hon. member carried on about withstanding pressures and about how one institution may have to compete with another institution, whether it be banks, trust companies, or insurance companies. He then commented on the purpose we should have in the legislation of protecting the interests of independents and of smaller concerns.
I would like to know the view of the Liberal Party. Very clearly in this proposed legislation there is protection for independent insurance brokers, of which we all have members in our ridings, in the municipalities we represent. We also have a tremendous number of car dealers throughout Canada. Each of us has one in our own riding. These brokers or car dealers contribute an awful lot to the community. Our proposed legislation has put in place protection to make sure that these independents carry on doing business and contributing to the communities in which they operate.
And the leasing dealers.

The car leasing dealers, absolutely.
I would like to ask the member opposite: Does the Liberal Party support the protection of these small, independent brokers and car leasing companies throughout Canada, or does it believe we should remove that from the bill and let the banks rule?
Government Orders

Well, of course not. I take my direction from the minister from my home province.
To go back to the question of Air Canada and Canadians, the reality is that it may be too soon to have an obituary; but it is not too soon to express concern about competition in that industry. To have two airlines essentially setting the pace and it almost being impossible for competitors to enter the market give us every reason to stand in this House and not wait until it is too late. I know the government would prefer to wait until it is too late, because then it can stand in the House and say that it has already happened and there is nothing it can do about it.
Of course we stand for the increased competition among independent insurance agents. Many families have built up multi-generational businesses through acting as independent insurance agents. They must be protected and therefore they must have products that they can put on the marketplace.
I do not know about you, Mr. Speaker, but the last time I looked the banks in Canada did not sell their products through independent agents. They sold their products through branches that they controlled. If we allow this system to continue, those branches will pick up every service they can. The principle behind this legislation, when it is finally passed, has to be to protect independent businessmen in every region of this country so that they can continue to survive.

Mr. Speaker, one wonders whether the hon. member for Ontario is representing the interests of Ontario in a national government which becomes more and more fractionalized, as we see through this legislation.
I wonder if I could draw the attention of my hon. colleague for Winnipeg North Centre who gave us a very thoughtful approach to the implications of this legislation, not only to competitiveness on a world scale but competitiveness in the four pillars of the financial sector, as he outlined. He also outlined what that competitiveness would do not only for the independents that operate in that business but, most important, the theme upon which he touched.
I noticed that the parliamentary secretary opposite a few moments ago suggested that the level of service, the quality of service and the security of service provided to depositors in trust and loan companies and banks should

October 30,1990
Government Orders
be the main focus of attention in this legislation. It should also be the type of regulations that will allow for the maximizing of opportunities that depositors and consumers would like to see from the four pillars of the financial sector.

Mr. Speaker, these issues are very important throughout the country, particularly in Manitoba. One of the last remaining independent insurance companies was Great West Life, which operated out of Winnipeg very successfully. Also the last remaining independent brokerage house in the country, Richardson and Greenshields, had its beginnings and its focus in Winnipeg.
And Wawanesa.

Yes, Wawanesa is another company. Winnipeg has a long tradition of building up financial institutions. Of course I know members from other parties who come from Manitoba would join with me in making sure that those companies remain strong and healthy through new legislation.
It is interesting how the changes sometimes go unnoticed, but I am sure the hon. member who just asked the question would be interested to know that in the last decade service charges in the banking system in Canada were introduced very quietly, obviously with the acceptance of the government. Canadian consumers now pay annually $3.1 billion, an average of $120 per person in banking charges. Those fees never existed before.
Isn't that disgusting? It is hard to believe it.

One of the greatest areas of expansion in banking profits in this country is from those services. We can see that if we allow that sort of development to continue without some questioning or without some movement on the part of the government to challenge them as to the need for this money, we will find ourselves to be victims again.
Consumers do not like their governments to be victims and to be feeling sorry for themselves. They like their governments to be strong, to show some purpose and to show some direction in protecting the consumer. Of course, as we see in the recent oil prices, the ability of the government to protect consumers is somewhat limited; but I am sure that the minister knows his responsibility and will be ever vigilant in protecting the Canadian consumer. That adventure is his commitment.
There are many other points I could raise, but I am sure the House wishes to continue so I will leave it at that.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have this opportunity to participate in the debate on Bill C-83.
First of all, I would like to congratulate the Minister of State for Finance for finally going ahead with this important process. As we know, we have had several papers in the past, but this minister has really started the process. He has taken a pragmatic approach and not a theoretical one.
The major objective, as I see it, is to make our financial institutions more competitive for the benefit of consumers. The world of financial services has been changing rapidly for a few years, and we must change.
The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Finance covered what I think of as the marketing side very well a few minutes ago. He did that very thoroughly.
Today I am going to deal primarily with the elements of ownership proposals affecting banks, trust and loan companies, life insurance companies, property and casualty companies, and the like of credit unions.
The federal government does not propose that a single ownership structure be imposed on all federally regulated financial institutions, or that a total ban on commercial enterprises acquiring any financial institution be enacted. The issue has been debated at length by parliamentary committees, industry associations, financial institutions and their owners. Arguments have been made in favour of both widely held ownership and closely held ownership and it is apparent that no ownership model is correct to the exclusion of all others.
The proposed legislation thus puts forward a pragmatic approach by allowing both forms of ownership to continue to exist within a strengthened regulatory environment.
Let me take a few minutes to discuss our bank ownership proposals. The proposed revisions to the Bank Act would permit chartered banks to be either
October 30,1990

widely held, on a path to wide ownership, or directly owned by a widely held regulated financial institution.
For Schedule I banks, which include the six largest domestic banks, the revised Bank Act would maintain the current regime of wide public ownership. Wide ownership of banks prevails in one form or another in all western countries and in Japan. The policy would ensure that the big six domestic banks would remain widely held with no one person or group of associated persons owning more than 10 per cent of any class of shares.
The existing Bank Act permits a Canadian or a group of Canadians to start a Schedule II bank and own it on a closely held basis for the first 10 years after receiving a bank charter. After that time, it must become widely held. This provision would be maintained in the new Bank Act.
As well, the new Bank Act would continue to permit a foreign bank to apply for permission to establish a foreign bank subsidiary in Canada, designated as a Schedule II bank.
In the new measure, the proposed Bank Act would expand the Schedule II bank designation to include banks that are directly owned by, and continue to be owned by, widely held regulated financial institutions that are not themselves banks, whether they be Canadian or foreign.
Owners of such a bank could be widely held trust, loan or stock life companies as well as mutual insurance companies or widely held securities dealers. As is currently the case for foreign banks that wish to establish banks in Canada, one of the factors that would be considered prior to giving approval for a widely held financial institution to own a bank would be the presence and nature of non-bank activities operated by the parent of the proposed bank.
If the ownership of a Schedule II bank subsequently changes as a result of a takeover or of the parent bank by an unregulated entity, for example, the Schedule II bank would be required to be widely held within 10 years. If it wishes to remain closely held, it could convert to become a federally incorporated trust company.
As to the ownership of non-banks, the trust and loan company bill and the insurance companies bill will permit federal trust, loan and stock insurance companies
Government Orders
to continue to be closely held and if sold, to be sold on a closely held basis.
A federal trust, loan or stock insurance company with $750 million or more in consolidated capital would be required, within five years, to take the necessary steps to ensure that at least 35 per cent of the total voting rights in the company are attached to shares that are widely held and listed for public trading on a Canadian stock exchange. A Canadian financial holding company or Canadian regulated financial institution could be eligible to meet the rule on behalf of its trust, loan or insurance company subsidiary.
Schedule I banks would automatically meet the 35 per cent rule by virtue of their 10 per cent ownership limit. The 35 per cent rule would not be relevant for Schedule II banks that are required by legislation to meet the 10 per cent wide ownership requirement within a 10 year period.
For other Schedule II banks, the 35 per cent rule would apply where a capital size of $750 million is reached because of the acquisition of a large domestic institution that, prior to the acquisition, was itself subject to the 35 per cent public shareholding requirement. A ministerial exemption from having to meet the 35 per cent requirement will be available for institutions that reach $750 million in capital through internal growth. Other situations, such as reaching the $750 million capital threshold through successive acquisition of a number of small Canadian financial institutions, would be examined on a case-by-case basis.
An extension of the five-year time limit would be possible where general market conditions warrant and the minister is satisfied that a company has used its best efforts to satisfy the rule.
The 35 per cent rule will ensure a significant public shareholding to provide a counterbalance to the influence of the majority shareholder. An element of broad public ownership can bring benefits in terms of ensuring market scrutiny and establishing the basis for sound, corporate government.
As for foreign ownership, the existing foreign bank regime will be maintained. However, the foreign bank guidelines will be modified to cover entry by non-resident widely held regulated financial institutions that are not banks, such as life insurance companies and securities dealers. In addition, the so-called 10/25 foreign

October 30, 1990
Government Orders
ownership rules now found in federal legislation, which limit acquisitions of Canadian controlled financial institutions by non-residents, will be based on a broader definition of control.
As part of the Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement, U.S. residents are not subject to the 10/25 rules. As noted previously, all significant changes in ownership of federal financial institutions will also be subject to the approval of the Minister of Finance, who will consider a number of factors, including the best interests of the financial system.
An ownership approval process is an important element of the proposed ownership regime. At present, the Minister of Finance has the authority to approve all start-ups of federal financial institutions, but subsequent changes in ownership do not always require approval. It is proposed that this deficiency be corrected by requiring that significant changes in ownership of federal financial institutions be subject to the approval of the Minister of Finance. This will ensure that a takeover is in the best interests of the financial system and that new owners have the expertise necessary to run a financial institution, adequate financial resources and sound and feasible plans for the future conduct and development of the business.
An investor will be required to obtain the approval of the Minister of Finance in order to buy shares of the financial institution that would result in the investor owning in excess of 10 per cent of any class of shares. Similarly, if an investor already owns more than 10 per cent of a class of shares and wishes to purchase additional shares, approval will be required.
Finally, an investor will be required to seek ministerial approval if that investor acquires control of a company that is linked to a financial institution and, as a result, there is a change in the significant ownership interest in the institution. For the ownership approval process, and generally throughout the legislation, control will be defined to include control in fact.
The proposed legislation will permit minor fluctuations in ownership to occur without requiring approval. As well, it will provide prospective owners with the
opportunity to obtain pre-approvals so that they can make business decisions with certainty.
As announced on August 11, 1989, the new legislation would make the approval process for trust and loan companies effective as of that date.
I believe the ownership proposals will work to the benefit of both the financial industry and its customers. I ask that we move forward quickly with the proposed legislation before us today.
As a long-time member of the finance committee I want to say that we are beginning to hold hearings. The member for Ontario might correct me, but I believe the deadline for submissions is November 15. We will be consulting widely with all people affected, auto leasing companies, insurance brokers, banks, trust companies, and credit unions, because this is an important milestone in financial services in this country. We do not intend to get bogged down. Yes, we will consult. Yes, we will take ample time. But, given how quickly the world is changing out there, Canada needs to be competitive.
I think we can be tremendously proud of our banks. When considering what is going on in the United States these days with the trouble that certain banks there have been getting into with bad loan portfolios, look at our banks. They are very sound. Some people might have been a little afraid of the free trade agreement, but our banks, which are class banks, are going to be even more competitive in the U.S. market.
Look at what is happening down there in the savings and loan industry. They are in trouble to the hundreds of billions of dollars. Even though they are closely held, look at the trust companies we have that have been so well managed.
Our life insurance industry, as well as the property and casualty, is not without some problems but frankly, due to the good management, good personnel, and also due to the very fine and thorough inspection by the authorities in Ottawa of their loan portfolio, capitalization rates, and so on, those companies have kept Canada in the forefront by being very sound financial institutions.
I take exception to any person who thinks that we are opening doors for weakened financial institutions. I think it is just exactly the opposite. I take great pride in being a part of this process. I wish it had started three years ago, but it did not. We are into round one and I
October 30, 1990

hope that all sides of this House will co-operate to enact the necessary legislation just as quickly as possible so consumers will have better deals out there and the financial institutions will be able to compete more effectively.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to ask the hon. member a question. When I look at a piece of legislation such as this, one of the questions I would like to ask is how does it helps the working man and working woman of Canada? Second, what evidence does he have that it will make us more competitive than U.S. banks, which is one of the points he has made? The answers to those two questions would be of great interest to me.

Mr. Speaker, I want to thank the hon. member for the question.
The Canadian banks in this country have approximately 7,000 branches, give or take a few hundred. They are about twice as well branched-if I could use that term-as banks in the United States. There is absolutely no risk that any U.S. bank-and mark my words, check it out in a few years-is going to come into this country and out-branch our fine Canadian system. Our banks have been well placed for years and will be able to service their Canadian customers very adequately, whether it is in a small town like Moose Jaw, Saskatchewan or in downtown Ibronto. I believe the American banks will concentrate more on the commercial loan aspect and other things. So I do not have any doubt there.
This proposal supports the organization of our fine insurance brokers, thousands across the country with small independent agencies, who give personal service and have that expertise. No American will be able to compete. No new American will come in on that.
There are thousands of auto leasing dealers across the country. It is a type of service requiring expertise and personal service. This legislation supports them 100 per cent and they will also be able to compete.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BILLS - MOTIONS   OFFICIAL LANGUAGES ACT MOTION FOR TABLING OF REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to inform the House about the government's actions to implement regulations under the Official Languages Act. There has been some concern expressed about the time it is taking to put these regulations in place.
In addition to the parliamentary committee on official languages, the Commissioner of Official Languages, representatives of the minority official languages associations and others have urged the government to take action. Now the government is asked to table the regulations as quickly as possible.
The government has been moving as quickly as possible to bring these regulations before the House. The suggestion that the government is not moving quickly
enough is based on misunderstanding about the process which must be followed.
In the 1988 Official Languages Act, Parliament set out in broad terms the course Canada will follow in official language policies and programs. The act sets out the right of the public to communicate with and receive services from offices of federal institutions in the national capital region and in other offices where there is significant demand for services in English and French and where the nature of the office makes it reasonable to provide these services in either language.
The act also sets out some veiy specific responsibilities, particularly for Treasury Board. The act directs that the Treasury Board take responsibility for the general direction and co-ordination of policies and programs for all federal institutions exclusive of Parliament for the implementation of the Official Languages Act. Treasury Board is also responsible for recommending regulations to cabinet. The President of the Treasury Board must present Parliament with a draft of any regulations that the Governor in Council intends to put forward.

Mr. Speaker, our government is anxious to consult the public before adopting regulations which are likely to affect them. A preliminary consultation seems the best way to ensure that the regulations are workable, fair and equitable.
In 1986, the government developed a policy for the drafting and publication of federal regulations. When dealing with such basic issue for our society as the official languages, Parliament took a number of additional steps by including in the Official Languages Act the process to be followed for the adoption of the regulations. That is precisely what we are doing!
If I may, Mr. Speaker, I should like to review the four main steps leading to the adoption of the regulations under the Official Languages Act.
The first stage is the most time consuming because all interested parties are supposed to participate into it.
To open the consultation process, the government publishes every year a statement of intention in its Federal Regulatory Plan, to inform Canadians of the regulations to be passed during the year.
October 30, 1990

In the case of the regulations made under the Official Languages Act, this document provides a short description of the general objectives and scope of each regulation.
As all hon. members probably know, a first series of consultations was held with representatives of both French and English communities throughout Canada to obtain their views on this matter. These consultations are compulsory under the Official Languages Act.
The proposals were then reviewed in the light of the views expressed in order to better reflect the needs identified during the consultation process.
Moreover, in keeping with the announcement he had made in this House, the previous President of the Treasury Board met with representatives of the two main umbrella agencies, namely the Federation of francophones outside Quebec and Alliance Quebec. He than knew for sure that no other propositions were better than the ones put forward.
Now that these preliminary consultations are over, the government can confirm to the members of this House that it is now ready to proceed with the approval of the proposed regulations as soon as possible and in the most appropriate way.
[English\
In the second stage of the process set out in the act, there is consultation with Parliament. This second stage, which is also unique, gives members the chance to study the regulations thoroughly.
To this end, the act says that the President of the Treasury Board shall lay a draft of the proposed regulations before the House of Commons. The act specifies that there must be 30 sitting days of the House before the draft regulations can be prepublished in the Canada Gazette. During the next 30 sitting days of both Houses of Parliament, the general public again has the opportunity to comment on the proposed regulations.
The regulations in draft form are made available to the public in Part I of the Canada Gazette which publishes them along with a description of their expected impact. The comments are studied. If they point out weaknesses or suggest improvements, the regulations can be changed.
Private Members' Business
Finally, the regulations are approved by cabinet and published in their final form with a final description of their expected impact in Part II of the Canada Gazette.

Mr. Speaker, the process I have just described is a long and complex one. But in this way all Canadians have the opportunity to express their views on the regulations. That is something nobody should object to.
The process which allows people to make their views known about the regulations is not the only complex criterion we have to meet in order to develop the regulations made under the Official Languages Act.
The regulations themselves are particularly complex.
In the case of the Official Languages Act, we need regulations to make sure the law is applied in a fair, reasonable, and consistent way. To meet this triple goal, we have to examine such concepts as "significant demand", "nature of the office" and "services to the travelling public".
Although mention is made on the Act some general criteria to define more specifically concepts such as "significant demand", the regulations have to take into account contingencies that may not, and should not, be set out in the Act.
As for the "nature of the office", the regulations must take into consideration, for example, the health, safety and security of members of the public, as well as the location and activities of the office.

Hon. members will appreciate that the regulations must be uniform and fair legal definitions, which can accommodate various circumstances in all parts of this country. Such uniformity and fairness is not achieved quickly.
We know that the Treasury Board secretariat has been hard at work for more than a year consulting with minority language associations and holding discussions with federal departments, agencies and Crown corporations.
Regulations are being drawn up which reflect the linguistic realities of Canada and which are fair. The government should not apologize for the time it is taking. The government should not be rushed into preparing regulations in haste. The government should

October 30, 1990
Private Members' Business
be given the chance to consult fully with interested parties.
The act ensures that all Canadians will have ample opportunity to comment on regulations that will contribute to a better service to the public across Canada.
I know that the government intends to propose regulations that are fair and reasonable. As a member of Parliament, this is an objective that I support. I trust that all members will lend the same support to these regulatory proposals once they have been placed before us.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is my understanding that in private members' hour now the rules that apply in ordinary debate do not apply and that you pick speakers as you see them.
Mr. Speaker, the motion presented by the hon. member for Ottawa-Vanier asks the government to table as quickly as possible the regulations necessary to implement the Official Languages Act of 1988 which was passed more than two and a half years ago.
Two and a half years have passed since this House voted on that bill and we still do not have the regulations. It is interesting to note that during that debate the Prime Minister stated that he was willing to have the House sit night and day in order to pass the legislation because it was essential for the country. Those were more or less the exact words of the Prime Minister.
Mr. Speaker, you will recall that the opposition to the bill at that time was not made by any of the opposition parties. The opposition came from certain members of his own party who were referred to by the press as dinosaurs. That opposition was there and the Prime Minister, wanting to get on with the business, said he would have the House sit night and day to pass the legislation because it was essential for the country.
I must ask what happened between those days in 1988 when the Prime Minister thought it was absolutely essential to get this legislation through and the two and a half years which have passed since. One wonders whether the dinosaurs within the Conservative caucus have grown in strength and have now more or less thrown obstacles in front of the government so that it does not have the political will to proceed with this legislation.
I refer to an editorial which was written in The Montreal Gazette of October 29, a few days ago, following the special report submitted to this House by the Commissioner of Official Languages. The headline in
October 30, 1990

the Gazette editorial states: "Languages law languishes. Ottawa's delays are letting the country down". Then it goes on to say: "Linguistic justice delayed is linguistic justice denied".
We not only have the promise of the Prime Minister during the debate to implement this legislation quickly, but the Commissioner of Official Languages has pointed out in his recent special report in which he condemned the government for not implementing the legislation a whole list of promises by ministers of the government that we were going to get the regulations soon.
On April 11, 1989, in answer to a question put by the hon. member for Ottawa-Vanier, the President of the Treasury Board said that the regulations would be tabled in the House before the end of 1989. That was a full year after the bill was passed. In any case, 1989 came and passed by, and we still did not see the regulations.
Then, on the first anniversary of the act, the Commissioner of Official Languages put out another press release on September 15, 1989 and asked what was happening, when were we going to see the regulations? Then again, in his famous annual report of April 3, 1990, the Commissioner of Official Languages felt he might have to resign because the government was in contempt of Parliament which had passed the law, and still there were no regulations to implement the legislation.
On the same day the President of the Treasury Board said that before June 23, before the summer, we would see the regulations. That was earlier this year.

The House adjourned at the end of June, the summer passed, and we still have no regulations. I might say that at the end of June the Standing Joint Committee on Official Languages issued a special report, a unanimous report, including Conservative members of the committee, Liberal members of the committee, New Democratic members of the committee, and senators from both parties, requesting the immediate tabling of the regulations to implement the legislation.

The House came back in September, and we still have not had the regulations. I raised the question a few weeks ago in an adjournment debate and the parliamen-
Private Members' Business
tary secretary came to the House and said: "Soon". Well, Mr. Speaker, soon is not good enough.
As a result, we see the Commissioner of Official Languages has once again condemned the government for its delays.
The minister, the parliamentary secretary and, again this afternoon, my hon. friend from Lachine have said that the reason is consultation. I have been in touch with the groups that were the subject of that consultation, and they say the consultation was over long ago.
When the Commissioner of Official Languages tabled a special report last week, he said in the press conference which he gave that he himself had been in touch with the groups, the Federation des francophones hors Quebec, Alliance Quebec, and the other francophone minority groups in the country, and they said that the consultations were finished. They do not understand what this talk is about consultation.
The reason is not consultation. We have no clear evidence. The reason appears to be a diminishing political will due to something that is happening within the Conservative caucus, but that is not reason enough.
While this delay has been taking place, we know that there has been a growing opposition to official bilingualism in this country, and that is unfortunate. Following the failure of the Meech Accord we have seen the growth of intolerance on both sides. Polls tell us that the majority of Canadians still favour official bilingualism, so the government should listen to those polls in this case. It should move ahead despite that growing opposition, but it is not showing the leadership.
The opponents to bilingualism are speaking out. I refer to groups such as APEC, the Association for the Protection of English in Canada, a unilingual, anglophone group which is anti-francophone, the Reform Party which has taken a position against the Official Languages Act, the COR Party, and certain Ontario municipalities which have passed resolutions against official bilingualism. That is on the anglophone side.
On the francophone side we have seen the Government of Quebec pass Bill 178, contrary to the court decisions at three levels in Quebec: the Superior Court

The other matter that he underlined-and he has much experience in this area and is worth listening to in the House-was that there is a growth of intolerance in Canada. The member and I sat on that Joint Senate-House of Commons Committee on Official Languages when APEC, the Association for the Protection of the English Language, came before it. We could see the intolerance.
As the member pointed out, there is intolerance both on the side of the French and on the side of the English. It is not restricted to one side. The member spoke out eloquently at that committee meeting and asked some pretty pertinent questions. He has always taken the position that we have to fight intolerance, whether it is English or French, anywhere in Canada. I just want to underline that I totally agree with him on that.
The question as he raised it at the end is-and if he had more time he could talk more about it; maybe I will-who is speaking for Canada? Who is showing some leadership for this country? Who is trying to bring it together?
I watched the Prime Minister in Question Period. He spends a lot of his time making cheap points. "Well, that belongs to the responsibility of the last Liberal government", or "I can quote from Jean Chretien who said" such and such, or "I can quote from Ed Broadbent" who said such and such, or "I can quote the member of Kamloops".
October 30, 1990

Those are cheap political points. I was ill at home last week in Vancouver so I watched television. I watched you on television, Sir, doing a superb job in your debut as deputy speaker. It is very interesting to watch this House for a bit. The Prime Minister should take a week off and go home and watch the House on television. Maybe he wouldn't be so smart-alecky and so quick to put down things rather than explain things to the Canadian people and show some leadership.
Let me deal with a couple of points in this debate. First of all, to the member for Lachine-Lac-Saint- Louis, the Conservative member who spoke for the government, I was going to say: Murder your speech writer, but that is a little too much. Take your speech writer out, he or she, and just hit them over the head a little bit. Wake him up. Get rid of it. Tear up the speech.
The hon. member is thoughtful and gives good speeches, but what an apology for bureaucratic inertia. It is one of the worst apologies I have heard. He said that the government has moved as quickly as possible. Is this moving as quickly as possible? This government makes a tortoise look like A. J. Foyt, the racing driver, it moves so slow. A tortoise moves quickly compared to this government.
Have you ever heard of Mackenzie King, Mr. Speaker? He used to be famous as a Canadian politician who always put off decisions. Sir John A. Macdonald, "old tomorrow" they called Sir John A. Macdonald. This government makes Sir John A. Macdonald look faster than a speeding bullet in making a decision, or Mackenzie King, because it simply is not making any decisions in this area.
The hon. member says that we are misinformed and that he will inform the House. It is not just us who are misinformed. Tell that to the Commissioner of Official Languages who does this job full time and is expert at it. He says that the government is dragging its feet.
What a pitiful excuse in that speech for bureaucratic dilly-dallying. He spoke of consultations and revisions. I made notes of this. Three times he spoke of revisions and he made four mentions of consultations, the first stage of consultations. Then there was the second stage of consultations, and no doubt there will be the third stage or the fourth stage.
Private Members' Business
MPs can study it and it can get in The Canada Gazette. It just goes on and on and on. The bureaucrats are fiddling while Canada is burning. We should get down on our knees and ask God, he or she, to say to the government: "For God's sake, show some leadership in this country".
This is not an unimportant area; this is a very important area. Let me just recap the motion and give a viewpoint from the New Democratic Party on this motion. The motion is that in the opinion of the House, the government should table as quickly as possible-

"As quickly as possible", in the other official language. [English]
-the regulations made under the Official Languages Act passed by the House of Commons on July 28, 1988 and promulgated on September 15,1988. This is October 30, 1990, and we are still waiting.
The background of the issue is as follows: Bill C-72 was passed in the House on July 20, 1988. The government has not presented the regulations required to put the bill into force. That is the way legislation like this works.
This spring, in the annual report of the Commissioner of Official Languages, there was a condemnation of the government for its failure to act. This matter was a principal issue at a hearing by the Joint Senate-House Committee on Official Languages.
Mr. Fortier of Alliance Quebec, the Federation des francophones hors Quebec and even APEC, the Alliance for the Preservation of English in Canada, participated.
Toute la gang was there.
Last week, Mr. d'Iberville Fortier, the Commissioner of Official Languages, issued a special report into the government's failure to enforce the Official Languages Act, 1988. He said in part: "If we want to make our country go on, the least we can do is make sure acts of Parliament are respected. Two years later this act still does not have teeth. These delays may well endanger the linguistic progress made in federal institutions over the years".
We may go backward as a result of not having these regulations. Mr. Fortier justified this extraordinary action, because it is, by noting that if the regulations were not tabled soon, providing 30 working days for Parliament to study them, they cannot be published-and the

October 30, 1990
Private Members' Business
member should listen to this-in The Canada Gazette. If the House prorogues, as this House might, we will have even further delays.
It is therefore fortunate that this motion has come forward for debate at this time. I congratulate the hon. member for Ottawa-Vanier for bringing it here.
I will not debate the substance of Bill C-72 or why the regulations are needed. I think the heart of the matter is why the government is not delivering here. What is, as Mr. Justice Oliver Wendell Holmes once called it, the inarticulated major premise? In other words, what is stopping the government? None of this gobbledegook that the member across gave. What is the real reason? This legislation has faced strong opposition from a number of groups who have never accepted the need and support for official language minorities, and have never accepted a bilingual Canada.
I think both these groups are represented within the Conservative caucus; nationalists from Quebec, and what my friend called dinosaurs from English Canada. It seems to me that the Prime Minister is afraid to take on these groups in the name of a higher cause, namely the unity of Canada.
I will give you an example of where the government is going. Tomorrow we are going to debate a bill on broadcasting. The government has withdrawn a clause which states that the CBC has to promote national unity, because national unity is a dirty word now for this government. I ask, where is the vision in this country of Henri Bourassa or Sir Wilfrid Laurier, who believed in a society of tolerance and believed in bilingualism from coast to coast where people at least had a right to be served and communicate with their government in their own language. That is all that the official languages does. It implements that vision, which is limited if anything.
I do not understand why the government is not bringing this in.

Mr. Speaker, this year we celebrate the 25th anniversary of the Royal Commission on Bilingualism and Biculturalism. The vision expressed in this report's recommendations have had a tremendous impact on the history of this country. The central recommendations of
the report, the principle that official languages minorities in Canada should be assured to get public services in their mother language, the idea that French as much as English should be a working language in Canada, were reflected in the Official Languages Act of 1969. The Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms is in the legislation in question today.

The government is celebrating the twenty-fifth anniversary of the Laurendeau-Dunton report on bilingualism by taking a step backward. The Prime Minister said these regulations wall be tabled at the most precipitous moment. For whom? When? It seems to me that there is a clear lack of leadership here.
Let me conclude by saying this. The government is endangering the whole policy of official bilingualism. The government is leading to more intolerance. It is growing in Canada on the part of the English and French and on the part of extreme groups like the Bloc Quebe-cois on one side and the Reform Party on the other. Who speaks for Canada? We need vision in the leadership of this country. Sometimes it is tough. Sometimes you have to face down the bigots. It is not easy to say that to some people in Canada. We want these regulations. We want them now.

Mr. Speaker, it is with great interest, as co-chairman of the Joint Committee on Official Languages, that I participate in today's debate. I would like to take this opportunity to mention the names of my collegues who talked sooner today, that is the members for Ottawa-Vanier, Notre-Dame-de-Grace and Lachine-Lac-Saint-Louis, because they are people with whom we work regularly in committee and who really strive to protect the interests of the French and English minorities in Canada. I believe we must recognize the good work done by my collegues on the committee.
The member for Ottawa-Vanier gives us the opportunity with the motion he presents today and which says: "That, in the opinion of this House, the government should table as quickly as possible the regulations made under the Official Languages Act passed by the House of Commons on July 28, 1988 and promulgated on Septem-
October 30, 1990

ber 15, 1988", to show how this government has fullfilled its obligations regarding official languages in this country.
Having been a member of the Joint Committee on Official Languages, the member for Ottawa-Vanier knows full well that these last few years, since 1986 or 1987, it is the minority groups who complain during the committee hearings that the law had become ineffective. It is a law on official languages, one must recognize, which was adopted in 1969 by the then liberal government, and which, over the years, has become ineffective.
I have a question for the member for Ottawa-Vanier, who strives so much to protect the interests of the French and English minorities in Canada.
For 15 years, he witnessed the ineffectiveness and the degradation of the Official Languages Act. Why did he not ask his government at that time to bring in regulations to give teeth to the legislation? No, Mr. Speaker, Canadians had to wait until 1984 when the Progressive Conservative government was elected. We promised major changes and reform of the Official Languages Act and we delivered. The Act was amended with the support of all parties in the House and with the support of all groups of society. The new act that our government put in place in 1988 was hailed by both the English and French media and by everyone else.
This means, Mr. Speaker, that when you talk about something, you have to put it in the right historical perspective. For 15 years, our linguistic minorities had to live under an act which had major flaws and shortcomings that we spent sitting after sitting denouncing at the Official Languages Committee. We acted and, as a result, we have an effective legislation. It is important to note, Mr. Speaker, that the absence of regulations does not preclude the application of the Act. This Act is in effect since September 1988.
Every French-speaking citizen living within an English-speaking majority and every English-speaking Canadian living in a majority French-speaking community is entitled to be tried and to work in the language of his
Private Members' Business
or her choice. Minorities have the right to equitable participation at work and have rights before the courts that they did not enjoy under the previous legislation, Mr. Speaker. At the present time, any citizen, with the help of the Commissioner of Official Languages, can lay charges against any federal institution or any organization that does not comply with the Act. Those are some of the positive aspects we included in the new legislation.
To get back to the motion of the hon. member for Ottawa-Vanier, on June 14, as Joint Chairman of the Joint Committee of the House and the Senate, I tabled, and I will read it to you, a report by our committee asking the government to produce its regulations as soon as possible, Mr. Speaker, and I may point out that according to Standing Order 109, the government has 150 days to do so. As the hon. member for Ottawa-Vanier mentioned, this period ends on November 11, and since November 11 is a holiday, as the House is aware, it means that the actual deadline is November 9. Personally, I am convinced the new President of the Treasury Board will table his response to our report by November 9, and that this response will involve the tabling, very shortly, of those long-awaited regulations.
I think the hon. member for Ottawa-Vanier mentioned that he respected and trusted the new President of the Treasury Board. Mr. Speaker, you realize he was sworn in on September 20, 1990, barely a month ago. When we consider the importance of his department, of the position of the President of the Treasury Board who has to look after the Public Service and all the departments in terms of their budgets and human resources, and when we consider that the new President has already given the new regulations some thought, I think this shows he is genuinely committed to going ahead with the regulations. Opposition members would probably have liked the President of the Treasury Board to hastily table regulations totally unknown to him as soon as he was sworn in. regulations totally unknown to him. Those who know the hon. member from Quebec City see him as a reasonable and responsible man who wants to have a thorough knowledge of the issues before he makes a decision. Is it to much to ask to give him a month to study the regulations we are about to table? I do not think so. In due time, the President of the Treasury Board will make his position known and I am sure it will be along the lines of the commitments made by the Prime Minister and our members to our official language minorities.

Private Members' Business
Mr. Speaker, 150 days may seem like a long time. Our report was tabled on June 14, and the government has 150 days or about five months to answer. Let us have a look at what happened since then. Our report was tabled on June 14. Two weeks after that, the House adjourned for the whole summer. We returned on September 24. We have been here for a little more than a month, Mr. Speaker. So chronologically, I think the two-year delay that has been mentioned can be explained easily in the light of what I have just said. Two years may seem like a rather long time, but above all it proves one thing, that there has been consultation, as the hon. member for Ottawa-Vanier said, even too much of it, but the fact we consult the population when we legislate has been one of the characteristics of this government.
Contrary to what Liberals did for a long time, we do not practise a policy of confrontation with the provinces and the Canadian society. We practise a policy of consultation and dialogue. Maybe we are making too many consultations, it is possible, but it is better to consult wisely in order to bring forth a beautiful baby, Mr. Speaker, a good regulation which will be long lasting and will satisfy the different official language minority groups in the country.
Mr. Speaker, I could speak at length of the consultation process, I could mention all the organizations- There are thirty-six associations for official language minorities in the country. They have all been consulted, and not only once, but twice, Mr. Speaker. The first time was during the 1989 summer, when the Office and Treasury Board officials drafted the first bill. We were determined to consult every one of these organizations across the country, to know for sure what they really wanted. Then, we took note of their demands and we went back to see them, Mr. Speaker.
Therefore, this shows how concerned and how serious the government has been about these regulations. Mr. Speaker, I see you are trying to tell me that my time has expired. Mr. Speaker, on April 3, 1990,1 rose in the House to ask a question of the Minister of Justice regarding gun control legislation in Canada.
When I rose in the House in April to address the urgency of gun legislation, the country was reeling in the aftershocks of the massacre at the Ecole Polytechnique in Montreal. Concerned Canadians were shocked and horrified by the senseless murder of young women by a man who should have been denied access to a firearm. Canadians across the country then turned their outrage and sorrow to action. On April 9,1990, a petition bearing the names of over 500,000 Canadians was presented to Justice Minister Kim Campbell. The message was clear. Canadians want tougher gun control legislation.
On June 26,1990, the Minister of Justice introduced a comprehensive package to strengthen the control of guns in Canada. The proposals provide a minimum waiting period for a FAC, a provision for two references who have known the applicant for at least three years,
Adjournment Debate
national firearms safety training courses, mandatory testing for would-be gun owners, and the establishment of a Canadian Advisory Council on Firearms.
The need for a balanced approach when dealing with the issue of gun control is essential. I want to make it clear that members of gun clubs are, for example, not the problem. I visited the Sharon Gun Club last fall and I was very impressed with their safety regulations. I do not want those good law-abiding citizens unduly harmed or inhibited by any gun control legislation.
For example, the proposal to limit the magazine or clip size to 5 and 10 for certain firearms is totally impractical. While it is important to recognize the rights of the responsible and legitimate firearm owner, legislation must deal harshly with criminals, gun dealers, and others, using or trading illegal or unauthorized firearms.
Stiffer sentencing, one of the important parts of the new proposed legislation, is essential to protect the public from attacks and murder by criminals. We should also consider additional years in jail if a firearm was used in a criminal act.
Since 1978 when tighter gun control legislation was introduced, the number of robberies, homicides, accidental deaths, and suicides involving guns have all decreased. There are about 1,400 firearm deaths each year. However, almost 85 per cent of these deaths were suicides. Homicides totalled approximately 180 deaths.
While these numbers tell us violent crimes involving firearms are decreasing, crimes still occur that could be prevented through tougher legislation. A case which I believe demonstrates the urgent need for tighter gun control laws is the attempted deportation of Robert Cave.
Robert Cave was sentenced to seven years in prison for several armed robberies in 1981, including the brutal and threatening attack of a 21-year old woman who was managing the McDonald's restaurant he robbed. This woman was terrorized by Cave who at the time was high on drugs. He shoved the nozzle of his pistol up her nose as well as using other threatening gestures. Robert Cave was given only two years for the use of a firearm in the commission of the robbery, in spite of his past criminal record and the obvious brutal way in which he used the weapon.

October 30, 1990
Adjournment Debate
Those convicted of an offence involving firearms should pay through hard time. We must make the country safe for all abiding and upstanding citizens. More care and compassion must be directed to the victims of violence.
There is another aspect of our justice system which must be changed in order to better protect our citizens. I am referring to our extradition laws.
Charles Ng fled the United States five years ago to escape prosecution and still remains in Canada. Charles Ng, a former U.S. Marine, was charged in California with the sex slayings of 13 people, allegedly committed between 1984 and 1985. In 1985, following a month-long international man-hunt, Ng was apprehended in Calgary after a bungled shoplifting attempt. Five years have past since his arrest in Alberta and Ng still remains in Canada fighting an extradition order thereby escaping prosecution in California.
I think it is possible that Canada could become a haven for criminals such as Ng, criminals who, facing the prospect of a death penalty, flee to Canada to escape prosecution. Because of Canada's close proximity to the U.S. and its long, continuous border affording many opportunities to flee, this notion is quite real.
We must not only toughen gun legislation but all legislation dealing with criminal justice. It is absurd to think that people such as Cave and Ng have more judicial options and opportunities available than does a Canadian citizen who is accused of committing a crime. Let us stand up for the right of all Canadians to live in a nation which provides them a sense of security and well-being. Our laws must provide more protection for society and a greater sensitivity to the victims of violence and their families.
In closing, I want to say that I held a town hall meeting in Stouffville last Saturday morning, October 27, 1990, to hear the views of the residents of my riding regarding the proposals to strengthen gun control in Canada. There were almost 40 people in attendance. I was assisted by three panellists: Norm Gardner, Vice-Chairman of the Metropolitan Police Commission; David Brown, a former police officer and a sports shooter; and Morton
Greenglass, a lawyer and legal expert on gun control and a sports shooter as well. A number of good constructive recommendations were proposed, and I will be presenting many of these to the Minister of Justice.
