speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, since I only have three minutes available to me, I will address the member's first concern, which is that of gun control.
I would like to say that the Minister of Justice shares the concerns of the hon. member. She is certainly aware of the strong desire among members of this House and the Canadian public for effective gun controls.
Gun control is a very complex issue. Many of our northern and aboriginal citizens, for instance, require firearms for their livelihood. We must try to balance the concerns of all Canadians about public safety with the legitimate interests of the responsible law abiding firearms community.
It should be pointed out that Canada already has one of the best gun control systems in the world. It has also been pointed out that more can be done.
It has been demonstrated that some types of firearms, those of a military nature, have become a problem since the law was last amended.
Bill C-80 represents a considered response to these concerns that will help assure the safety of the Canadian public with the least possible interference in the interests of legitimate and responsible gun owners.
The previous Minister of Justice, who is now Minister of Transport, had the benefit of extensive consultations with the provinces and many firearms interest groups during the summer of 1989. The present Minister of Justice intends to pursue the consultation process as the bill proceeds through Parliament. In particular, the Canadian Advisory Council on Firearms is being set up to give members of the firearms community and other interested parties access to the consultation process.
The intent of the amendment proposals is to address a number of concerns that have arisen since the law was last amended in 1978. Some of these have to do with the screening of applicants for firearms acquisition certificates and other documents.


October 30, 1990

Adjournment Debate
It should be kept in mind that some types of firearms present a risk because they have a design or firepower that cannot be justified with any legitimate or socially useful purpose in mind.
Our problem is to make a distinction between those firearms that have a legitimate sporting and hunting purpose and those that do not. This is what Bill C-80 attempts to address.
I can tell the hon. member that the consultation process that was begun by the prior Minister of Justice will continue. I am looking forward to this piece of legislation getting into committee so that we can hear some other concerns of Canadians who have taken an interest in this area.

Mr. Speaker, I rise today to give a little further information and perhaps a little more in-depth questioning on a question that I asked in this place on October 2.
I asked two questions. I am not sure to which one the parliamentary secretary will be responding this evening, but I am going to address both those questions because that is what I put in for.
The question I raised that day dealt with the advance collection of the goods and services tax. The particular case in point was a lady in Halifax County who had prepaid a ticket to Florida, and the travel was to take place in April of next year. She was absolutely astounded when Air Canada called her back and indicated that she not only had to pay in advance of the ticket, which she fully expected, but she also had to pay in advance the 7 per cent goods and service tax. That lady was incensed, as she should have been. She called my office, she went to the media and she said: "This act is not yet law and not only is it not yet law, and the government and the bureaucrats will come up and tell me reasons why they can still collect it, but my goodness, it is facing the fight of its life in the Senate of Canada". Eight-five per cent of Canadians have consistently been opposed to this form of taxation. Surely to goodness the government is not going to tell consumers across this country that they have a legal obligation to pay that 7 per cent goods and services tax in advance of January 1 or whenever that act becomes law. Hopefully it never becomes law.
I asked the Minister of National Revenue if he would give us an unequivocal statement, to stop trying to dance around the issue, on whether or not he had instructed businesses across Canada that they had no legal obligation to demand from a consumer that tax be paid in advance of January 1.
With the glibness and smugness of this Minister of National Revenue, he got up and said: "No, I won't because I have done that on August 9". If he did it on August 9, he certainly should have done it again the day I asked because in the next few days the media was full of reports of outraged consumers from coast to coast in this country who had been told by this government that they had to pay the 7 per cent goods and services tax in advance. The minister likes to have it both ways.
This government has spent over $30 million. It is a lot of money, hard-earned money that has been taken from the taxpayers of this country, $30 million to put out propaganda, some of which has been found to be false and misleading by the Advertising Standards Council of Ontario dealing with this proposed, wonderful great thing that the government is trying to foist upon the Canadian public called the goods and services tax.
Instead of doing his job, the Minister of National Revenue refused in his next propaganda mail-out to big, medium and small business in Canada to tell those businesses that they had no legal right to collect in advance the goods and services tax. He did not want to come forward and do what he should have done under the law and tell those businesses that they had no right.
My second question that day was to the minister who was supposedly responsible for consumer interests, the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs. I said: "My goodness, are you going to do the right thing? Are you going to do what your job is and protect the interest of consumers and ensure that they know that they have no legal obligation to pay in advance the 7 per cent goods and services tax?" He was mute. He was silent. He was in the House that day but he was mute and he allowed it to go back over to the Minister of National Revenue.
I am going to tell you, Mr. Speaker, it will be a sorry day for consumers in this country when it is the Minister of National Revenue who is looking after the interest of

October 30, 1990
Adjournment Debate
consumers. It is supposed to be the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs, but, again, that minister did not do his job, not just for the lady in question in Halifax county who found it repugnant that she was being forced to pay a 7 per cent goods and services tax on the advance purchase of airline tickets, but for every consumer in this country.
I asked that day in my supplementary question to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs how he could in all good conscience have sat at the cabinet table and allowed the government, the cabinet of the day to approve expenditures, a multi-million dollar series of expenditures to put out propaganda to the Canadian public, to the consumers of Canada which he knew to be false and misleading. If he did not know at the time, he should have listened to the Advertising Standards Council this summer when it said that the radio ads that were paid for, not by members of the government, anybody out there who is watching, but by your tax dollars. The government was trying to fool Canadian people and do it with their own money, for goodness sakes.
I asked the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs that day whether he was prepared to do the right thing and dissociate himself from the propaganda campaign of this government. As I said, he remained mute.
The Canadian public has not decided that they are going to lay down and die on the goods and services tax. The latest poll that is out, it was just one poll. I guess I could not quote it with a great deal of authority, but it is one of a series of polls that have been done since this government embarked on that dangerous path for Tory-dom called the goods and services tax. Every single poll that has been taken regionally or nationally shows that this government is out to lunch in its pursuit of the GST. Maybe if the government was supported by 51 per cent of Canadians, but 85 per cent did not like the tax, you might say, "Well, maybe it is a passing fancy".
The numbers speak for themselves. Seventy-five per cent of Canadians in the last poll that was done said that they were absolutely, fundamentally opposed to this regressive, crazy, insane tax, called the GST, particularly
at a point in time when this government's policies have driven the economy of the country into recession.
The only lower approval rating for any issue that was in the poll was for the popularity of this government. Only 15 per cent of the respondents said that they supported this band of rascals opposite in their pursuit of fiscal and social policy.
It becomes clear that this government has lost the moral authority to pursue policies that are not supported by the majority of Canadians. I would hope that I am going to get a better answer tonight from the parliamentary secretary, as he licks his lips waiting to get up and give us the answer.
I want to know from the parliamentary secretary why is it that the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs did not look after the interests of consumers? Second, why is it that the minister responsible for Revenue Canada, since he is sending all kinds of propaganda out saying what a great tax this bad tax is, did not tell the businesses of Canada that they did not have a legal obligation nor a right to collect this tax. Why, if it was so complicated, did the government not forego that little bit of tax that would have been paid in advance for the first two or three months of next year and protect the interests of the consumer, and, for once, protect the interests of Parliament and the parliamentary process?

speakeroldname: Mr. Vincent Della Noce (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Revenue):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Revenue
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will answer on behalf of the Minister of Revenue but not on
behalf of the Minister of Consumers and Corporate Affairs.
I would now like to give a more detailed answer to the questions asked by the hon. members for Dartmouth and Scarborough West about the requirements under the proposed GST that apply to businesses getting paid after August 1990 for goods and services to be received after December 1990.

Let me first say that, in advance of Bill C-62 receiving Royal Assent, collection of the GST for transactions straddling the transition date is strictly voluntary and is suggested as a matter of convenience for the consumers
October 30, 1990

and the businesses involved. In fact, under the legislation, the vendor will not be required to remit any GST collected until the first GST return for 1991 is due.

On August 9, 1990, the Minister issued a press release to remind businesses of the interim provisions of Bill C-62. This release stated that businesses supplying goods and services to be delivered after 1990 will be accountable, effective January 1, 1991, for the proposed 7 per cent GST on advance payments made between September 1, 1990 and January 1, 1991.
Even though the Minister was urging businesses to follow the interim regulations contained in the proposed legislation, he clearly stated that, in these cases, collecting the GST on the 1991 part of the contract was not yet mandatory.

The decision on whether to charge or pay GST on invoices issued on or after September 1, 1990, for goods or services to be delivered after 1990 is a matter for vendors and their customers to decide. However, I can appreciate that in many instances this would be the most convenient and least costly approach to take.

To conclude, Mr. Speaker, the government is continuing to emphasize that there is no legislative authority to enforce collection of the GST until the legislation is effective. At the same time, we will continue to encourage businesses to be prepared to account for the tax due on prepaid supplies.
If I have 10 seconds left, Mr. Speaker-

I will repeat the last paragraph in English for my colleague.
To conclude, Mr. Speaker, the government is continuing to emphasize that there is no legislative authority to enforce collection of the GST until the legislation is effective. At the same time, we will continue to encourage businesses to be prepared to account for the tax due on prepaid supplies. Mr. Speaker, I hope that answers my friend's questions.

Mr. Speaker, on October 17,1 pointed out to the Minister of Employment and Immigration that refugee claimants in Canada, who
Adjournment Debate
have already been hurt by their experiences that caused them to seek refuge in Canada, were studied in a survey by a team of church people, under the direction of psychiatrists, and 58 per cent were found to be in deteriorating mental health. Their mental health was worse since they came to Canada than it was when they arrived.
Why? One of the reasons is the difficulty in getting jobs. They cannot get a work permit until the first hearing, which is often delayed. Even then, it is often a limited work permit and, even then, employers say: "Well, we do not know if you are permanent here because you have not had your second hearing". There is anxiety about their futures and, worst of all, there is separation from their families. Usually husbands and fathers here are separated from their wives and children overseas.
One man came to my office two weeks ago who had been here six years. His wife died overseas, while waiting for him to bring her here. His children wrote to him and said: "You have killed our mother, now you are going to kill us. Why will you not bring us"? There is nothing he can do. This government will not let him have his case decided, and will not let him bring his family here until his case is decided. Even after his case is decided, he must wait a year for landing and then wait some time after that for the processes of immigration.
I asked the minister what steps were being taken to end this torture, this misery. All she could say was that 50 per cent of the cases have been opened in the refugee backlog. After 21 months, since the program was announced, 50 per cent have been opened. Not 50 per cent resolved, 50 per cent opened. She did not give us any indication whether they will really be able to finish it on time, a year from now, as they promised.
I asked her for an amnesty. I have never asked that of the minister before but, because of this terrible situation, I asked her to land all the people in the backlog so long as they meet the health and security standards which are required by the legislation.
There are many, many of those people who are skilled, many of them who have one of our official languages, and they are able to settle readily. Whether we consider that they were cheaters or whether we consider they were real refugees, it is time to stop torturing them and it is time to stop breaking down the immigration system by pouring staff into that useless project. Expensive staff, adjudicators, translators, lawyers, and so on are having

October 30, 1990
Adjournment Debate
their time wasted while the minister pursues that project.
The Canadian Council of Churches presented this matter in a brief to the United Nations Human Rights Committee, under article 40 of the Covenant on Civil and Political Rights. It was reported today in The Globe and Mail that the UN committee was very concerned about what Canada was doing. The council pointed out to them that Canada is now giving priority to processing claims of English-speaking applicants from the Caribbean, forcing many applicants from other countries of severe persecution to wait years before their claims are handled, and they can attempt to bring over family members.
The UN committee expressed, and I quote, "grave concerns about Canada taking people out of order, by virtue of language, and processing their applications first". An expert Toronto lawyer, Ms. Jackman said, and I quote:
-a study by the inter-church committee shows that "people become suicidal" when they are in limbo for five or six years without a determination on the outcome of their refugee application.
The brief proceeded under four articles of this covenant. One is there should be "no cruel or inhumane treatment" and "committee members suggested that these long delays to people who had already suffered trauma could be a form of cruel treatment". That is article 7. Under article 14 of the covenant, everyone shall have a "fair trial, committee members expressed concern that delays were not consistent with a fair trial and questioned the independence of the Immigration and Refugee Board".
Under article 23, protection of the family, "committee members were concerned about delays in reuniting families". Under Article 26, against discrimination, the committee members asked questions which "left no doubt that singling out English speaking Caribbean claimants was to be viewed as discrimination".
Today, the minister denied that that is being done, but I have spoken to many people in Toronto and I find that church representatives and lawyers in private practice- this government usually likes private practice rather than government. It wants to privatize everything but it attacks the lawyers in private practice if they do not kowtow to the government.-are finding that their
clients are having their cases set back if they are not from the Caribbean in order to move Caribbean cases ahead.
It is also being observed that most of those who are currently being processed are black. I ask: What is the government trying to do? Is it trying to juggle its statistics, that is, rush through these hearings and a lot of deportations? Or, is it trying to punish people who it considers cheaters en masse because of their country of origin? In so doing, it hurts real refugees whom it claims to be trying to protect. It also delays Canadians who want to sponsor their families into Canada but are delayed because the experienced immigration officers are stuck working on the backlog.
I ask that the minister consider an amnesty.

speakeroldname: Mr. Bill Kempling (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Employment and Immigration
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to expand on the reply given by the hon. Minister of Employment and Immigration to the hon. member for Trinity-Spadina on October 17 of this year.
The minister rejects the notion that this process is torturing refugee claimants. Refugee claimants in Canada enjoy the protection of Canada while their claims are being determined. In fact, as Gordon Fairweather, the Chairman of the Immigration and Refugee Board has pointed out, a United Nations high commissioner for refugees has said that within the Canadian refugee determination system there may be a model for the world.
The Minister of Employment and Immigration understands the concerns of backlog claimants who are waiting for decisions. That is why steps have been taken to make that wait a productive one for claimants. Backlog claimants have had permission to work since January 12, 1989. They and their families have access to Canadian schools and social programs.
The Minister of Employment and Immigration also understands the concerns of backlog claimants who are separated from their families. That is why measures have been put in place to bring to Canada on a priority basis the dependants of backlog claimants who are facing life threatening situations or who are abused or abandoned children. In addition, as soon as a claimant has been provisionally approved for landing, the appropriate visa office is requested to initiate processing of the dependants the claimant intends to sponsor. This reduces the time required to bring those dependants to Canada.
